en: Ūṃ.
[Now begins the Śivādvaitamañjarī. Salutations to the venerable Guru Basava-liṅga. [Now the work titled Śivādvaitamañjarī is being written.]
May there be auspiciousness.
I bow to Śrīnātha, the peaceful one, free from the three guṇas, the sun that dispels the darkness within the hearts of his disciples;
he who resides upon my head in the white lotus at the end of the twelve, arising within the triangle of the lotus.

In the [triangle] consisting of three excellent lines called Will, Knowledge, and Action, [and] joined with the phonemes *ha* and *kṣa* (according to another reading: "joined with the phonemes *ha*, *kṣa*, *la*, and *ra*), in the Bindu which is oriented toward all phonemes, [He is] endowed with the two feet of Vision and Action, which cause the arising of both Consciousness and Unconsciousness. || 1 ||

The non-duality of Brahman, which is beyond the conceptualization of a self, is proclaimed by others; yet that very [non-duality], through its divisions such as existence and so forth, comes to rest most clearly within duality.

Having established that method and having presented the multitude of refutations against [other views], and having demonstrated that it is Brahman which possesses true vision and action, we declare that this entire universe is of the nature of that Brahman. || 2 ||
Therefore, the beautiful cluster of the non-duality of Śiva (Śivādvaitasumañjarī) shall exist through the exposition thereof, which is the very foundation of the universe.
Therefore, let this work, which is appropriately named after that [deity], grant satisfaction to those who possess devotion to Śiva. || 3 ||
In this regard, indeed, those who maintain the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādin*) among the followers of Vyāsa describe the intention of the *Vyāsasūtras* as follows: To explain:

Since it is established that the mutual existence of the "you" and "I" cognitions— the object and the subject— is impossible due to their contradictory natures, like darkness and light, the mutual existence of their respective attributes is even more impossible; therefore, [the Self] is the subject, the conscious self, which is the object of the "I"-cognition.
The superimposition of an object— which is the sphere of your cognition— and its attributes upon the subject, and conversely, the superimposition of the subject and its attributes upon the object,
ought to be considered false; nevertheless, through mutual non-discrimination, one superimposes the nature of each upon the other, as well as the attributes of each.

This natural worldly transaction—“I am this,” “this is mine”—arises from false knowledge by coupling the real and the unreal, [the latter] being the utterly distinct nature and its possessor. It is asked:
what is this so-called superimposition (*adhyāsa*)? It is replied: it is the appearance, in the form of memory, of something previously perceived elsewhere. That...

Some say that there is the superimposition of one thing upon another; others, however, maintain that where there is the superimposition of one thing upon another, that error is based on the non-apprehension of their distinction;
yet others hold that where there is the superimposition of one thing upon another, it belongs to that very [thing].

They describe it as the conceptualization of a nature possessing qualities contrary to that [object]. In every respect, however, the appearance of the qualities of one thing in another does not fail to occur;
and thus there is experience in the world: for mother-of-pearl appears as if it were silver.
And how can there be superimposition of objects and their attributes upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is not an object—such that "one moon appears as if it were a second"?
For everyone indeed superimposes one object upon another object situated before them;
yet how can the inner self, which is associated with the notion of "thou" (*yuṣmat-pratyaya*) and is projected by that notion, possess the status of being an object?

You say this; it is replied: this [Self] is not, however, absolutely beyond the scope [of cognition], because it is the object of our own cognitive awareness (*asmat-pratyaya*) and because the inner Self (*pratyag-ātman*) is established through its immediacy (*aparokṣatva*). Nor is there this restriction that another object must be superimposed only upon an object situated directly in front.

Even though space is imperceptible, the ignorant superimpose its surface, impurity, and so forth upon it; in the same way, the superimposition of non-selfhood upon the inner self (pratyagātman) is not contradictory. Scholars consider this superimposition, characterized as above, to be ignorance (avidyā), and they call the ascertainment of the true nature of reality through the discrimination of that [superimposition] knowledge (vidyā).
This being so, that upon which there is superimposition is not affected by even the slightest quality or defect produced by that [superimposition].
It is presupposing this very mutual superimposition of the Self and the non-Self, known as ignorance (avidyā),
that all worldly and Vedic transactions involving means of knowledge and objects of knowledge proceed, as do all [scriptural injunctions and prohibitions].

Having established the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) with the passage beginning, "The scriptures are intent upon injunctions, prohibitions, and liberation," and ending with, "Thus, this beginningless and endless natural superimposition, consisting of false cognition, which impels one toward agency and enjoyership, is evident to all the world."
Having established that the entire phenomenal world, as characterized by means of valid cognition such as perception, is the object of ignorance (avidyā),

and having made the formal proposition— preceded by the distinction between the insentient and the sentient— that all Vedāntas are commenced for the realization of the knowledge of the oneness of the Self in order to abandon this cause of misfortune;
In order to fulfill that very proposition, this treatise, consisting of four chapters,
has been expounded as being dedicated to the non-duality of Brahman devoid of distinctions.
In this regard, it is considered: what is the proof for the existence of ignorance (avidyā)?

Is it perception (pratyakṣa), or inference (anumāna), or perhaps scripture (āgama), or an internal experience? It is said that although it is not perceptible to the eye, its existence is established through the fact that the visible effects [of the world] would otherwise be inexplicable, as in the scriptural passage: "Knowledge and ignorance" (vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca).

If it is argued that there exists some positive entity called ignorance (*avidyā*), which is beginningless, indefinable, based upon Brahman, and directed toward the individual soul (*jīva*), as determined by scripture and by the experience "I am ignorant," then [we ask]: by what means is such a proof established for that ignorance?
And [by what means is] that ignorance [itself established]? By what [means] is such a proof [established]?

If it is asked what [the means] is for the word "siddham" (accomplished), [the answer] cannot be "by means of knowledge" (*vidyā*), because that would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Furthermore, is there difference (*bheda*) or non-difference (*abheda*)? Not the first, because since the nature of knowledge consists in being distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*), its means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) must necessarily be of the same nature as that knowledge; consequently, it would follow that those three [ignorance, its object, and its means] are real. Nor can it be [known] by that means of cognition—
It cannot be argued that there is no fault because difference is accepted on the grounds that [the object] is an effect of ignorance;

for if there were a difference between cause and effect, it would be impossible to maintain the alternative of either identity or difference regarding the object which serves as the cause of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in its form as an effect. Thus...

For [if they were different], there would follow the consequence of [the clay] not being the cause [of the jar], due to having a distinct nature like that of a thread and a jar; nor can it be said that [this] is possible [in the case of clay and jar] as it is in the case of a thread and a jar, because clay and jar are devoid of absolute difference—[otherwise] there would follow the consequence that [clay], like the thread, would be the primary cause. Therefore...

Because the illustrative example is dissimilar, one should not argue that— just as in the case of threads and a jar— although there is no difference in the distinction between clay and a jar, it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that clay alone is the cause of the jar.

For one must investigate what the basis is for that causal relationship between clay and a jar, which is established through such positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Nor should it be said that the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) and so forth is itself the regulator, because one must likewise investigate what the basis for that [concomitance] is, just as in the case of threads and a jar.

Since there is also a specific distinction between difference and non-difference even in the case of clay and a jar, one must, having no other recourse, take refuge in the very coexistence of difference and non-difference (bhedābheda) between clay and jar; and this is not something undesirable for you. Nor should it be argued that because difference and non-difference are contradictory, their coexistence cannot be accepted.

Because the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) is more powerful, it is impossible to avoid the conclusion that "only clay appears in the form of a jar," and thus the notion that "the jar is made of clay" (*mṛd-ghaṭaḥ*) cannot be denied; for if one were to say "the jar does not exist," one would be unable to account for common linguistic usage such as "a pot is born from clay."
Because it would follow that the act of arising, which is established in the present time, would be without a substratum—

since the jar does not exist at the moment of its birth and thus its production is impossible— it must therefore be admitted that the causal capacity for the effect does not reside within the causal substances such as clay and the like.
Since an absolute difference between the staff and the jar is impossible,
one must accept their non-difference in a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*); otherwise, by the example of the staff and the jar,
there would be no cessation of the effect even upon the cessation of the ignorance that serves as its cause.

Therefore, since the relation of cause and effect is impossible without accepting both difference and non-difference between them, and since difference-and-non-difference cannot be sublated, and because, according to the reasoning stated, it is impossible for that which is distinct from knowledge (vidyā) to possess the nature of knowledge or to be its effect; [therefore, the world is non-different from Brahman].

(–) This point was obtained from another work: since it is impossible to distinguish between "effect" and "cause" when they exist as a single nature, and because difference and non-difference cannot be accepted due to their mutual contradiction, for that very reason even the analogy of the clay and the jar is cast aside; if, on the other hand, only difference is intended—then...

Because identity (tādātmya) is impossible, even when the cause—avidyā—is removed, the cessation of its effect, the phenomenal world (prapañca), would not occur, just as a jar remains even when its cause, the staff [that supported it], is destroyed. If one were to accept this consequence (iṣṭāpatti), liberation itself would not exist, because bondage is included within the phenomenal world. Nor is the second alternative tenable.

Because there would be no distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), such that one could say "this is the means of knowledge" and "this is the object of knowledge," due to their non-difference;
for if it were itself the means of knowledge regarding its own existence, it would follow that it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

(If it is argued that this is acceptable because it would entail the fault of self-dependence: Since it appears independently of anything else, like the Self itself, no one engaged in worldly transaction desires a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its own existence. If that [self-dependence] were also accepted, then it would be nothing but knowledge (*vidyā*); there could be no talk of "ignorance" (*avidyā*), nor would even knowledge exist therein.

It cannot be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because, being stainless, it is devoid of any coloring by objects; since it is this very [consciousness] that is ignorance (*avidyā*), its manifestation is impossible. Therefore, one must seek a means of knowledge for the existence of ignorance.

Furthermore, even on account of the consequence of [the world] being twice as real, the acceptance of ignorance (*avidyā*) is not possible, because one must accept that there is no such thing as ignorance apart from Brahman; nor can it be argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because it is the very existence residing in the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that appears in ignorance and its effects.

It must be stated that, while ignorance exists, does that existence appear when it is real or when it is unreal? From this dilemma, the first alternative is not tenable, because [the object] already exists in the form of being and thus requires no further connection with another existence; nor is the second [tenable], because [existence cannot belong to] the non-existent.

It cannot be argued that the aforementioned defect does not apply because ignorance is neither existent nor non-existent, owing to the contradiction between existence and non-existence and the impossibility of its connection with existence; for even if it were characterized as such, the same previously mentioned defect would persist upon the alternative analysis of whether it is real or unreal in that form.
Now, even if ignorance is somehow admitted, the relationship of locus and located between Brahman and ignorance is not possible,
because of their mutual opposition, just like light and darkness; nor is it the case that light and darkness coexist everywhere, as in the case of the eye-light of an owl being pervaded by darkness.

It must be stated that, because there is no contradiction, it is possible in that same way; for it is recorded in the *Saptaśatī*: "Some living beings are blind by day, while others are blind at night; some living beings have limited vision both by day and by night."

Because his vision is limited and overwhelmed by the brilliance of the sun, he lacks the capacity to perceive objects of knowledge; otherwise, since he would be devoid of the perception of objects such as the moon and its light even at night, he would be perpetually blind, and the designation "day-blind" (divāndha) for him would not even be possible. Nor is this situation possible according to the analogy of the moon's spot.
Since Brahman is partless and devoid of distinctions such as upper, lower, or lateral divisions,

if there were no contradiction between those two [ignorance and the vision of reality], then ignorance would not cease even through the vision of reality, precisely because of that lack of contradiction;
for it has been stated that "action does not remove ignorance because they are non-contradictory."
Furthermore, it would follow that Brahman is ignorant, like a house enveloped in darkness; nor can this [ignorance] exist even partially, because Brahman is partless (*niraṃśatva*).

Even a distinction of parts imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) is impossible, since no prior state of such imagination can exist, and because there is no location external to Brahman at all. This is according to the reasoning already stated.
Because of the impossibility of stability.
Furthermore, indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) is also not possible, because it is determinable (*nirvacanīya*) by virtue of being an insentient entity (*bhāva*) that is beginningless (*anādi*).
Nor is its beginninglessness possible, because—like a jar or other objects—it possesses parts and is insentient (*jaḍa*), and thus cannot be established through itself;

if such self-establishment were admitted, it would follow that it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). If, on the other hand, it were established through another (*parataḥsiddhatve*), [it would be dependent].
Because, like a jar or other such objects, it would follow that there is an infinite regress by way of seeking another cause due to its being an effect;
furthermore, its nature as a positive entity (bhāvarūpatva) is not possible because it is characterized by the meaning of a negation (nañ);
nor is its being the material cause (upādānatva) of the universe possible, because it is insentient (jaḍatvena) and devoid of its own existence (svasattā).
And because there is an absence of impelling power; for since the conscious principle is devoid of attachment, such impelling is impossible.

Nor should it be argued that the causality of ignorance is possible through the proximity of consciousness, as in the analogy of the magnet, because proximity is necessarily restricted to two things situated in different locations.
By that analogy, since there is no location external to Brahman, [the Māyā] resides in Brahman itself;

yet, like a needle that has entered a magnet, because it is devoid of independent activity, the action of transforming into the form of the universe is impossible. If it were to produce an effect without any support at all, then—
Due to the consequence of attaining independence, it would become unavoidable; if such a consequence were accepted, liberation itself would not exist.

Furthermore, it is not possible for that [knowledge] to have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its object; for while the [knowledge] is insentient and thus an object, the individual soul is sentient and cannot be an object—hence the contradiction. Even if this were accepted, since the heart of the individual soul is overwhelmed by ignorance (*avidyā*), there would be no discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things, nor indeed...

Neither from the perspective of the teacher nor from the perspective of the scripture is [ignorance] established; for even the teacher has a heart overcome by ignorance, and the scripture, being an effect of ignorance, is of the same nature as it. Therefore, there is a lack of evidence for the existence of ignorance; even if it were accepted in some way, it would result in the fallacy of dual reality.
Because of the contradiction between Brahman and ignorance, like light and darkness, the relationship of locus and located is impossible;
and because if there were no contradiction, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator would be impossible, it would follow that Brahman is ignorant and that ignorance lacks beginninglessness.

Because it is impossible for Brahman to possess the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*), it is impossible for it to be the impeller [of the world]; for that very reason, it is impossible for it to be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe, impossible for it to have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its object, and because if that were accepted, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things would be impossible; therefore, O Śarva, [this knowledge is taught] for the sake of abandoning this cause of misfortune.

The statement that the Vedāntas are being commenced is indeed improper; the point is that since the Vedāntas and their commencement are of the same nature as ignorance (avidyā), they are not in opposition to it, and therefore it is impossible for them to be its remover.
Now, the definition of superimposition (adhyāsa) stated as "having the form of memory and appearing as something previously seen elsewhere" is not possible;
for instance, because it is observed that a snake previously perceived in an external location such as an anthill is superimposed upon a rope present in front of one, so too is it here.

Because there is no region outside of Brahman, and because one never observes in the world the superimposition upon a thing of what has been seen only there; for instance, in the illusory attribution of yellowness to a conch shell, the yellowness must have been seen elsewhere, otherwise the cognition "the conch is yellow" would not arise,
since yellowness had not been previously perceived [in the conch].

Otherwise, there would be no distinction at all between error and valid cognition, because that which is perceived in one place would be admitted as being in that very same place due to superimposition (*adhyāropa*). Nor should it be said that being sublated by a subsequent moment constitutes error,
for even the shell and the silver are equally real entities, just like a jar and a cloth.
Because the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is impossible, there is no sublation of the cognition of silver by the cognition of mother-of-pearl;

for, like the cognitions of a jar and a cloth, those two [cognitions] have different times and different objects. Otherwise, the cognition of a cloth would also be sublated by the cognition of a jar. Nor is it the case that "this is not silver."

It must be stated that the subsequent cognition "it is indeed mother-of-pearl" is called the sublater of the previously arisen cognition of silver; likewise, for a cognizer who, after the cognition of a jar, abandons the jar and perceives a cloth,
the certainty "this is not a jar, it is a cloth" is also [the sublater] of the previously arisen cognition of the jar.

It would be subverting because every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists of a determination preceded by the negation of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Nor can it be argued that, due to their having different substrates (*bhinnadharmikatva*), there is no contradiction between such conceptual constructions and thus no relationship of the subverted and the subverter; for in this case, however—

Since it is impossible for two contradictory appearances— namely, "this is silver" and "this is not silver"— to both possess validity with respect to a single substratum (dharmin), one must admit that the cognition of silver produced earlier is sublated by the subsequent cognition of the absence of silver.
Because the relationship between the sublated and the sublator depends on mutual connection— like the maxim of the staff and the vessel—

and because that [connection] is absent due to the two being at different times; for, according to the rule that cognitions persist for only three moments, at the moment the cognition of the absence of silver arises...
If it is argued that because the cognition of silver produced earlier— which has reached a state of perishing— is still present,
a mutual connection between the two is possible, we say no; for since cognitions are qualities (guṇas),
there can be no mutual connection between them either through conjunction (saṃyoga) or inherence (samavāya), due to their insentience (jaḍatva).
And because it is devoid of such orientation [toward an object], the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is simply not possible.

However, just as for a cognizer who has abandoned a jar and perceives a cloth, there is the closing of the cognition of the jar and the opening of the cognition of the cloth by the power of his will, so too— in respect to a single substratum (dharmin)— by virtue of proximity...

This is because the two cases are equivalent: for one who perceives specific qualities such as a blue back, there must be admitted to be the cessation (*nimeṣa*) of the previously arisen cognition of silver due to distance and other factors, and the emergence (*unmeṣa*) of a subsequent cognition that "this is not silver, it is merely mother-of-pearl."

If it is argued that being erroneous (*bhrāntatva*) consists precisely in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogyatva*), we say no; for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even eternal non-existent entities (*nityābhāva-padārtha*), such as a sky-flower, would be erroneous, since they too possess the capacity for causal efficiency.

If even those were considered erroneous because of their capacity for causal efficiency, then [the cognition] "this" [with respect to a shell-silver] would be like [the cognition of] shell-silver and so forth.

It would come within the range of visual perception. Furthermore, since the rule for word-formation applies even to things such as "sky-flowers," one must indeed accept their substantiality (*vastutva*) due to their connection with a compound formed by the capacity characterized as "unification of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), by virtue of the science of grammar (*śabdānuśāsana*). This is because the Creator’s creation of the fit and the unfit is diverse.
Because it is based on the varying degrees of the imagined nature of the shell [as silver] through its own autonomy,
and because of the Śruti, "The real and the unreal became the Real," and the Smṛti, "I am both being and non-being, O Arjuna," everything indeed has Being-Consciousness-Bliss as its essence.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "of the object and the subject, which are the respective spheres of the notions of 'you' (yuṣmad) and 'I' (asmat)," even the distinction between the insentient and the sentient produced by that [notion] is not possible.
For instance, just like pleasure and so forth which are experienced apart from the notion of "I," [the same would apply to] its object.

If it is argued that [the self] is inferred because its being the object of the notion "I" cannot otherwise be explained— given that some things are invisible and our notion is false— then since the inferrer himself is also invisible,
that consciousness he intends [as the self] is, for all intents and purposes, like the son of a barren woman.

Because it has been stated that the inner self (pratyagātman) is well-known due to being the object of the notion "I" and because it is immediately present, such [an objection] is utterly trivial. Furthermore, it is not possible for that which is the object of the notion "you" (yuṣmat-pratyaya) to be insentient; for when a dispute arises between Caitra and Maitra—
Because, by virtue of their mutual causality, only a cognition having "I" as its mode is perceived;

because [the Self] has consciousness as its object, whereas the insentient is the domain of the notion "this"; and because of the authority of such scriptural evidence as "He created all this" and "This body, O son of Kuntī, is called the field. What [more is there to say]?
If the "Thou" (tvam) were an object of cognition for an insentient entity, then the instruction "That thou art" (tattvam asi) would be addressed to the insentient alone; therefore,
since both the "Thou" (tvam) and "I" (aham) cognitions have consciousness as their single object, one who argues that— even though one should say "this am I"—
the use of the second-person pronoun (yuṣmad) is intended to indicate an absolute difference, is thereby refuted.

And because those two have absolute non-difference due to having consciousness as their sole object, [it was said] by the Blessed One: "Never indeed was I not, nor you, nor these lords of men; and yet we shall all certainly not cease to be hereafter."

Furthermore, because the three persons— known as the third (uttama), middle (madhyama), and first (prathama)— are all subsumed within the "we" (*vayam*) through their inclusion in the notion of "us" (*asmat*), for this very reason, the relationship of object and subject cannot exist between the objects of the notions of "you" (*tvam*) and "I" (*aham*), due to the absence of any difference in nature, since consciousness cannot be an object for another consciousness.
Because it would follow that [the self] is insentient, like a jar or other objects within the domain of consciousness.

Nor should it be argued that this rule does not hold because the validity of the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) with respect to the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) is admitted; for since the primary cognition rests upon the cognizer, knowledge— unlike a jar or other objects—
is never perceived as "this is [knowledge]," and thus it always transcends the status of being an object of cognition (*prameya*).

Since both the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) and the reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) have the jar alone as their object— because the reflective cognition consists in making the jar, as manifested by the primary cognition, present to the heart of the subject, in the form "this jar has been known by me"— otherwise, one would have to admit that another jar [as the object of the primary cognition] is also the object of the validity [of the reflective cognition].

If it is argued that, because the pot delimited by "pot-ness" is always [present] as "this" residing in the word *prameya* (the cognizable), and because there is never an absence of its transcendence [from that state], another pot is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to a [given] pot— then this is equally applicable here as well;
for since knowledge ultimately rests upon the knower, [it is always present] as "this."
Because it lacks the status of being included within the category of the object of cognition (*prameya*),

therefore a relationship of subject and object (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is simply not possible between two things of the same class. Otherwise, there would be no distinction at all between "means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and "object of cognition" (*prameya*), even in the case of a valid cognition (*pramiti*) which is itself of the nature of a means of cognition.
Because [the self] is admitted to be an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*),

and because it is also admitted that "valid cognition" (*pramiti*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), likewise, it is not possible for the self to be an object of knowledge, because it is the knower (*pramātṛ*). Otherwise, if it were also an object of knowledge, [it would follow that it is not the self].

There would be the consequence of infinite regress due to the dependence upon another cognizer, since the distinction between the object of cognition and the cognizer is constituted by difference. For this very reason, contradiction between the objects of the notions "you" and "I" is also impossible, because they are of the single nature of consciousness; there is no contradiction, just as there is none between light and darkness, if [they were so].
By way of secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is precisely this nature of being the object of the "this-cognition" (*idaṃ-pratyaya*) that is intended [by the term *idam*].

Even so, because that which is insentient (*jaḍa*) and within the scope of the "this-cognition" appears as mounted upon the light of the Self—such that one says, "It is observed by me" or "It manifests to me"—there is no contradiction between those two. Thus...

There is no contradiction even between light and darkness, because both of them appear by depending upon the self-luminosity [of the Self]; otherwise, if there were a contradiction between them, their very manifestation would not occur. This is also supported by the Śruti: "By His light all this shines; everything shines after Him as He shines. Nor...

The mutual existence of these two is untenable, because it must be admitted that the object of cognition (prameya), by means of the act of cognition (pramā), ultimately rests upon the cognizer (pramātṛ) due to the otherwise inexplicability of memory. If it is argued that memory arises from latent impressions (saṃskāra) alone, [we reply] that even those impressions, by virtue of having an object, must likewise rest within the self. Nor can there be [memory] of a jar that was never experienced...

It cannot be argued that memory— which takes as its object a thing previously experienced— arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) merely by virtue of being accompanied by a state of being an object, since the repose of the self in the form of "having perished" is impossible; for objectivity (*viṣayatā*) is a property of the object, and [memory] cannot exist without it.

Because their coexistence is impossible; for if the identity of those two were not established, then the cognition "this is a jar" would not arise, since [the jar] would be external to the light, like darkness outside of light. Nor can it be argued that its status as an object of illumination is possible in the manner of a jar external to light, because [it is] the Self.

This is because of such scriptural passages as "Space was produced," and so forth; for, according to the analogy of the clay and the jar, since each subsequent element is the effect of each preceding element, there is an identity between the two through that causal series.
Furthermore, [this applies] even in the case of being delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
It cannot be argued that [the connection] is impossible because consciousness resides only in the region of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),

while consciousness delimited by an object resides only in the region of that object, and thus there is no relation between the two; for [consciousness] exists in the form of the three Vedas (*traividyāṅga*).

Even though there is a state of complete merging (ekalolībhāva) between consciousness delimited by the modification (vṛtti) and consciousness delimited by the object, there is no such merging for the embodied self (śārīraka) delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) with the consciousness delimited by the object;
because the internal organ is subject to transformation (pariṇāmin), it is impossible for it to go outwards along with [the self], due to the difference in location (pradeśabheda).

Even if a distinction is perceived due to the difference in consciousness, since cognition is a quality of the self, it lacks any contact— whether by conjunction or inherence— with substances that possess qualities belonging to another;
thus, because objects such as blue cannot be its objects, it is impossible for cognition to possess objectivity.

And thus, according to the aforementioned reasoning, because their own scripture would result in futility due to being devoid of the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, and because such qualified aspirants (adhikārins) would be absent— therefore, in that view,
there is a lack of distinction between the insentient and the sentient.

Precisely for this reason, because the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is impossible, and precisely for this reason, the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation is as non-existent as a flower in the sky; therefore, the embodied being (*śārīraka*) qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), who is the intended candidate (*adhikārin*), lacks the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities with respect to Brahman.
Because this light is devoid of distinctions, one rejoices in it as the supreme, internal, non-objective, and non-sequential self-existence; yet, because it is empty of manifestation—
being insentient like the light of a crystal or similar objects— it follows that the sublation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) must be accepted.
Because this would result in the subversion of the promise made in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad that through the knowledge of one thing all things are known;
and because, in the passage "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman," it is specifically the attributeless Brahman that is designated as the object of inquiry.
Furthermore, the definition of the world’s origin and so forth as being unique to that [Brahman], which was stated in the immediately preceding sūtra, would also be inconsistent;

for since that [Brahman] is devoid of agency and other such qualities, the authors of the treatises do not accept the statement of a definition for a category of entity that has not been previously introduced. For this very reason...

In brief, because the subsequent operation of the scripture beginning with "Because it has the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt) is thus blunted, that which was stated [by the opponent] should be disregarded by learned authorities.
If this is so, how can the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda) be sustained?
For you do not admit ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of false cognition which serves as the material cause of the universe;
furthermore, since Brahman is changeless, transformation is impossible, as it would entail defects such as being subject to modification.

If it is argued that the acceptance of another external material cause for manifestation is simply impossible because it contradicts the doctrine of non-duality (advaita), then this must be reflected upon as follows: Consciousness (prakāśa) is the agent of the act of becoming; that very same [consciousness] is the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the act, existing both in its own state and as perturbed.

According to the position of the Sārasvata-sūtra, "The Heart is the All-pervading Expansion"; and based on the Vedic scripture, "One should know that Heart as the great abode of the universe," it must be accepted that the Light of the Self— which serves as the foundational wall for the phenomenal world of moving and unmoving beings— exists.

Otherwise, the world would fall into blindness; for there is the consequence of the loss of its own existence, as the Śruti declares: "He becomes non-existent if he knows Brahman as non-existent; if he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing. Furthermore, because it is the very basis of all, [the Śruti says]: "Other beings live on only a fraction of this bliss."
Since the act of becoming has its locus solely within the manifestation of the sensitive heart (*sahṛdayaprakāśa*), it possesses an agent;
and if that very act, being established in itself, rests solely in consciousness and bliss, then [the thought] "I rejoice" occurs within this manifestation.
[This is] the reflection: otherwise, there would be the consequence of insentience, like the light of a crystal and so forth.

If it is agitated—that is, if it is oriented toward creation—it is seen, according to the position of the Brahmasūtra "But it is seen," just as the production of a scorpion and the like occurs from cow dung and the like.

She consists of the manifestation of the manifold universe, comprising the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth. For it is said: "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, consisting of knowledge, strength, and action, and being innate. This is due to the wonder of the particle *ca* ("and"), which illuminates the meaning not explicitly stated in that Vedic passage.

Because the supreme power (*parāśakti*), which constitutes the very nature of Maheśvara, is understood to possess manifold forms such as consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action; and because desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, [and so forth...]
Since the scripture states, "Fortitude, lack of fortitude, shame, intelligence, and fear—all this is indeed the mind," desire and the other qualities are attributes of the mind;
therefore, one might ask: how can they be the nature of the Self, given that they are experienced as residing in the body?

Furthermore, since the Naiyāyikas and others accept that even for a bodiless Lord, qualities such as desire and so forth exist, it would follow that [the Lord] is no different from jars and other such objects. Moreover,
because there is a rule of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the desire to know and bondage and liberation, [the agent must be] the mind characterized by those [states].

Or else, there would be the undesirable consequence of liberation [for everyone], because both [the bound self and the liberated self] would be equally false. Furthermore, it cannot be said that "desire for knowledge" belongs to one characterized by bondage while "liberation" belongs to its qualified substrate (the self), because that would entail a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*) due to the identity between the qualified entity and its substrate being false.

Because [desires] are incapable of liberation; therefore, since there is no contradiction in accepting that the intent of the scripture (*śruti*) is to demonstrate the manifestation of desire and so forth from the artificial knower (*kṛtrimapramātṛ*) through the mind, and because it is understood from another scriptural passage— "In Him all desires are contained"— that these are the very nature of the Self (*ātmasvabhāva*) by virtue of the natural force of the word "completely" (*samyak*).
This being the case, there is never any agitation (*vikṣobha*) in Consciousness (*cit*) and Bliss (*ānanda*), because their nature is non-sequential (*akrama*).

This is because the powers of Will (*icchā*) and the rest possess both sequential and non-sequential forms, and thus are subject to agitation. Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction between the sequential and the non-sequential; for such a claim involves a self-contradiction (*vyāghāta*), as it would imply a contradiction between difference and non-difference.

Since it must be stated that [the contradiction] is known only after [the two terms] have been known, because both the distinct and non-distinct forms of the objects appear in that cognition, and because that [cognition] possesses an object;
otherwise, the manifestation of the contradiction itself would not occur. Therefore, of the manifestation...

Furthermore, due to the absence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), there is no contradiction between difference based on mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and identity; for we do not assert such a difference, because it is impossible, since in that case "otherness" could not be established as the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a category (*padārtha*), which would lead to the absurd consequence that a category would be other than itself. Nor is it the case that...
It should not be argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because the nature of a category consists in its difference from other categories;

for since that [nature] is constituted by particulars, it is not the subject of the question, whereas only the "difference" that enters into the general definition of difference is the subject of the question. Furthermore:

The uncommon cognition that "the nature of the cloth is its difference from the jar" and "the nature of the jar is its difference from the cloth" is only possible once the difference between the jar and the cloth has been established;

thus, since that [difference] remains something yet to be desired [established], [it cannot be proven by such cognitions]. Nor can it be [proven] by [the properties of] being composed of threads, being made of clay, and so forth.

It should be stated that this is because the difference between those two is established; for even the certainty that "the jar alone consists of clay" and "the cloth alone consists of threads" occurs only after the difference between the jar and the cloth has been established.
Furthermore, this applies to the states of consisting of threads and consisting of clay as well.

Difference [of objects] arises from the difference of their parts, and the difference of those parts arises from the difference of their own parts; thus, when one investigates down to the limit of atoms, because they are partless and beyond the reach of the senses, there is no apprehension of difference therein. Consequently, since this would lead to a root-destroying infinite regress (*anavasthā*), [the theory of difference is untenable].

Nor is there any other limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) based on difference, because since difference itself is merely a product of imagination, it would lead to fallacies such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Rather, we maintain that difference is simply division, according to the analogy of gold and a bracelet. In that case, [the claim] that "the bracelet is not gold" [is false].
Because it is impossible to avoid [this objection], and because we observe that one who desires gold engages with the earring; thus,
it is improper to maintain that "gold never becomes an earring," since it possesses the suitability for being an earring and because it is precisely gold that appears in the form of an earring.

It cannot even be said that "the golden earring does not exist," because in common usage such as "the earring is produced from gold," there would otherwise follow the absurd consequence that the act of production—occurring in the present time—would be without a substratum; for at the moment of its birth, the entity, such as the earring, is not yet present. Therefore, it exists.
If [it is argued that it exists] because of the impossibility of its arising and because of its persistence:
even if one accepts the persistence of a presently arising entity despite the absence of persistence for an already arisen entity, then—

due to the aforementioned fault— the impossibility of its persistence arises either because it is manifest (*vyaktatayā*), or because it is unmanifest (*avyaktatayā*) through its non-difference from its own cause.
Because the existence of objects such as earrings and the like must be admitted.

This being the case, since there is no contradiction between the non-difference [of Brahman] and the difference that serves as the basis for its manifestation, and because [the latter] depends upon that very [non-difference] by virtue of being differentiated from it, it is— by the power of the skill of the artist— in the specific painting, like the appearance of an elephant and a bull, or like the serpent and the earring of Brahmā, [manifested] through its own independence.
Because it manifests in the form of power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), and for that very reason it is conscious; for in the word "conscious" (*cetana*),
the suffix has the sense of a state (*bhāva*), and thus it manifests the meaning of the verbal root as an unmanifested action, [which is] action.
Because the agent who is its substratum is also implied by that very [act] through the rule of having a substratum;

because the action contained therein is of the nature of an act (*kṛti*); because an act has an object; and because, being of the nature of consciousness, the act is self-luminous—due to this power of independent self-manifestation.

Because its nature is solely that of light. For this very reason, since division is preceded by conjunction, and because there is an absence of any relation between Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca)—due to Brahman being devoid of the phenomenal world—there is no room for the blemish of doubt that a difference of manifestation is impossible; thus, [the text] quotes the scripture: "Not here, not many."
Because the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is intent upon the elimination of worldly duality;

because it consists of the essential identity of all things; because its abiding in a state of differentiation is impossible; and because it does not depend on any relation such as inherence (*samavāya*) or conjunction (*saṃyoga*), nor does it admit of categories such as quality (*guṇa*) or possessor of quality (*guṇin*).

Because inherence is impossible, and because conjunction is preceded by action— since conjunction arising from the action of one or both [of two objects] is only possible when they are situated in different locations— it follows that such [conjunction] is impossible here due to the absence of any location external to Brahman; for a conjunction not preceded by action is unestablished.
From this, the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs are born.
Space, air, fire, and water—these six are the sustainers of the universe.
Thus, because of this scriptural authority, and because space and the other elements are included within the category of effects,
even the example of the conjunction of an atom with space is discarded; for it is not established for either disputant, as [space] is always the bearer of subsequent weight.

Because it would entail the loss of independence, and because a relation, being unitary and partless, cannot reside in two things; for if it were to have parts, it would follow that it is a substance, and as such, it would require another relation by virtue of its being a relatum.

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of infinite regress if one were to seek [a further cause] by way of investigation. The scriptural passage beginning with "without parts" (*niṣkala*) intends to convey that [Brahman] is devoid of any separable, material, or inferior elements (*kalā*); otherwise, it would follow that it is insentient, as it has been indicated that, like the luminosity of a crystal or similar objects, it would lack self-reflective awareness (*nirvimarśatva*).

Therefore, because Brahman is conscious, it is not like a corpse; for the Śruti declares: "He thought, 'Shall I have no companion? He desired a second. He was so great. Having created that, He entered into it. Having entered it, He became the manifest and the unmanifest. And as it is said: "Like in the world, His activity is solely for the sake of sport."
And because of the existence of the Brahman-sūtra, if the creation of the universe for the sake of His own play were dependent upon some cause other than Himself—

like a potter and so forth— then, through the dissipation of His orientation toward Himself, He would become dependent on other factors such as the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) due to His orientation toward something else.

Because it would otherwise follow that [the yogi] lacks sovereignty, the yogi— like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and the like, which bestows desired objects without depending on any cause other than itself, and like a spider (*ūrṇanābha*)—
[manifests effects] through identity (*tādātmya*), according to the principle of the diversity of colors such as feathers and legs found within the fluid of a peacock’s egg.
By virtue of being the nature of the pervasion of consciousness, by virtue of being the nature of vibration characterized by autonomy, by virtue of being the nature of the radiance of consciousness,

by virtue of being the nature of the nourishment of consciousness, and by virtue of being the very form of consciousness, [the Self] encompasses the five elements beginning with space, which have attained identity with the orb of the stainless mirror of one's own Self and are embraced by the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Having diversified the universe— which consists of both the insentient and the sentient, characterized by the fourfold nature beginning with the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—
by means of the chisel of *apohana* (the power of exclusion) which is the form of His own will-power,
[He manifests it] as the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth.

The established conclusion is that [the Lord] plays while being a connoisseur of the great drama characterized by the fivefold functions of creation, maintenance, dissolution, bondage, and liberation; for since the power of will possesses an object, its manifestation would be impossible without the universe abiding within it.
Now, if the existence of the universe is admitted through its non-difference from Brahman,

then because it is eternal, the bondage contained within it would likewise be eternal; consequently, since its cessation would be impossible even through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), liberation would not occur, and there would be the undesirable consequence of bondage persisting even for one who is liberated.

If it is argued that because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) undergoes the six kinds of ontological change (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*), Brahman— being non-different from it— would consequently be subject to impermanence, it is replied: in the statement "the pot perishes," the action of perishing cannot reside in the pot by its own nature alone.
Because destruction is impossible; because the instruments (karaṇas) are dependent upon the operation of time; because those [instruments] depend upon the organs of action (karmendriya);
because those [organs of action] depend upon the organs of knowledge (jñānendriya); because those [organs of knowledge] depend upon the internal organ (antarendriya);
because that [internal organ] depends upon the artificial subject (pramātṛ); and because that [artificial subject], being subject to space, time, and so forth, lacks autonomy.
Since it cannot exist without [the cause], its subsistence in that [cause]— being defined by it—

must be accepted even against one's will; and since the agent is Maheśvara by nature, one must accept, according to the direction shown, that effects such as earrings exist in the form of their causes, such as gold.
Since the persistence of the effect as the essence of its cause constitutes the destruction of that effect, there is no entailment of defects such as mutability; for in the case of milk and the like,
the action of transformation is observed to depend upon time, instruments, and an agent, and thus possesses the nature of an agent.
Furthermore, since even qualities and defects possess the nature of a single self-essence,
in the world there is no total abandonment of one's own defects in all transformative objects; for instance,
when a transformative substance such as gold undergoes transformation into the form of an earring.

Since the abandonment of forms such as gold and so forth is directly experienced, and because even a trace of modification— such as the transformation of an independent entity— is impossible according to the maxim of the contraction of a tortoise’s limbs, action indeed finds its rest only in the object (karman) and not in the agent (kartṛ).
Nor does liberation follow from logic.
Beings have an unmanifest beginning, O Bhārata, and a manifest middle.
Their end is indeed unmanifest; what lamentation can there be in that?

Thus, according to the statement of the Blessed One, because the prior and posterior limits— characterized by worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*)— are one's own true nature (*svasvarūpa*) due to the universe being of the single essence of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*), they lack any obstructive power; and because,
like a jar or other objects that have entered the sphere of desire and so forth, they are devoid of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), [the obstruction exists] only in the middle limit.

"Because it is characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it is an obstacle. O Goddess, for that wise man whose conceptual cognition—which consists of the means of proof and takes the form of 'the knower' and 'the known'—arises as fashioned by you, his own nature remains unstained by it; yet, there is no liberation for him. Thus it is stated by Kālidāsa in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*.

Since the will of the Lord alone is the regulating factor, there is no possibility of the liberated soul being bound again; thus, there is never any logical inconsistency. This should be reflected upon by learned scholars whose hearts have been purified by the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*).

This being the case, in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa established in the first sūtra that Brahman alone exists, based on the scriptural passage: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second; it thought, 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" according to the etymological derivation of the verbal root *īkṣ* as meaning both "to see" and "to intend."
Because it is vast (*bṛhat*) by virtue of being distinct from the insentient due to its nature of seeing characterized by perception,

and because it possesses the characteristic of the agency of independent seeing— which is of the nature of bliss consisting in the volition for the act of becoming many in the form "May I become many"— it is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is seeing.

And because it has been played upon [in the Upanishads]. Since Brahman—characterized by independence in knowledge and action—is designated as the object of inquiry, the definition of its unique attributes, such as the origination of the world, mentioned in the immediately following sūtra, is also appropriate.
For instance: "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (atha ato brahma-jijñāsā). Herein, [it is said]: "The Self, indeed, my dear, should be seen, should be heard..."
"One should reflect upon it, one should meditate upon it" is the subject sentence (*viṣayavākya*).

The doubt is whether the scripture (*śāstra*) is not to be commenced or is to be commenced. [The prima facie view is that it is not to be commenced] because [the Self] has been proclaimed in this world and in the Veda as "Puruṣottama" by the Blessed Lord himself in the *Gītā*. Here...
Worldly renown is not established by means of inference, because commoners and others lack knowledge of the necessary pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other such logical requirements.

Rather, it is known even by children through the realization "I am"; thus, even in the Veda: "I am Brahman," "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," and "I am the first-born of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*), the navel of immortality before the gods."

Because of such scriptural passages, Maheśvara is well-established; since he is beyond doubt, he cannot be an object of inquiry. Furthermore, because the ignorance (avidyā) residing in the individual soul (jīva) is of the same nature as Brahman, its cessation is impossible, and because there exists no other entity external to Brahman.

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that the scripture should not be commenced, because produced bliss is to be rejected due to its impermanence, and because eternal bliss is neither something to be attained nor has it ever been attained; therefore, there is no purpose [for the scripture].

It is true that "I" (aham) is well-established as Brahman in both cases; nevertheless, in this world, among those outside the Vedic fold who are discerning proponents of the doctrine of consciousness (vijñānavādins), there exists no eternal intelligent being whatsoever— neither a creator of that consciousness nor a Lord (īśvara)— in view of the continuum of momentary cognitions.
They say this because, while their cognitions are distinct, there is no evidence for their existence as external to cognition;

for if there were such evidence, since it would necessarily be included within cognition, they would be identical to cognitions, just like jars and other entities. Thus, even regarding Vedic matters, the followers of Kapila [cite] the scripture beginning with "the unborn" (*ajā*).

Because it is heard in scripture that *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is the cause of the universe, they assert that there is no Lord (*īśvara*) whatsoever apart from *puruṣa* (the individual soul) and *pradhāna*. The followers of Jaimini, however, maintain that with respect to heaven characterized by pleasure, only rituals such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* are enjoined; [the attainment of heaven occurs] solely through the force of the unseen merit (*apūrva*) residing in the sacrificer, which is produced by those [rituals].

Because it is possible for those things that serve as the means to achieve [that end] to arise, they argue that the Vedāntas are concerned with the agent, the deity, and the substance; since they possess purposefulness through their utility for ritual performance, they are merely remnants of ritual action (*karmaśeṣa*) and not concerned with Brahman.
For this very reason, there is disagreement even regarding the Veda among various classes of disputants.

The established conclusion is that this scripture must be commenced for the sake of attaining liberation— characterized by the expansion of the power to be described hereafter— by means of refuting the various heretical doctrines, both Vedic and non-Vedic, that have entered [into discourse].
And thus, the meaning of this Sūtra is as follows: now,
for the qualified seeker who has acquired the means such as tranquility and self-control through the power of virtuous deeds like the worship of Śiva accumulated over many births.

After the manifestation of the power of an extremely intense desire for liberation, [it follows that] because rites such as the worship of deities other than oneself— characterized by sacrifice (*yāga*) and yoga— as expressed in passages like "Therefore, henceforth, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), are to be abandoned due to their impermanence, as evidenced by scriptural texts such as "This world acquired through action perishes" (*eṣa karmacito lokaḥ kṣīyate*). Therefore, of action...

Because [the self] is insentient, it is devoid of the effort to produce what was previously non-existent; and because the deity consists of sound, it is likewise insentient; for that very reason, the means and the fruit [of action] would be like flowers in the sky; and by this same logic, the Sāṃkhya doctrine which asserts the Pradhāna as the cause is also refuted—[this is the conclusion] of the Vedāntas.

Because it is read in a distinct section, it is devoted to Brahman by virtue of the six marks that determine its purport; and because the self-reality accepted therein is manifold and characterized by mutual exclusion, it consequently rests solely upon the specific nature of its own respective objects.
Because one is almost as if blind and deaf with respect to the objects and essential natures of others,
there occurs a mutual discernment of difference— such as "Caitra is distinct from Maitra" or "Caitra is happy while Maitra is suffering"—
regarding the manifestations of Caitra and others that have been differentiated, such as "I know Caitra" and "I [know] Maitra."
Because there is no possibility of internal synthesis through the attachment of a single cognition such as "I know," since the manifestation "I am Caitra" illuminates only its own self as its object.

Likewise, even for those who accept a momentary consciousness as the self—a view not sanctioned by the Vedas—there is a plurality due to its appearing in various forms such as blue and so forth; consequently, the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by it are likewise manifold. Because they reside in different moments of time, they are devoid of mutual connection. For this very reason, according to the aforementioned reasoning, each impression resides solely within its own object.

Because it is, as it were, blind and deaf with respect to the objects and essential natures of others, [the self] exists through its adherence to a single consciousness (*eka-saṃvit*) in such forms as: "Blue is different from yellow; yellow is different from blue; I know the blue"; and "I, who previously experienced my parents in childhood, am that very same I who now experience them as having perished."

Because the connection between the external and internal is untenable due to the absence of any intervening consciousness that could grasp both moments, and because the vibration of the prāṇa-vāyu characterized by rejection and appropriation exists even during states such as deep sleep.

Because that [sleep] is preceded by an agent— that is, preceded by the cognition of an agent— and because for one who has awakened there is a recollection of pleasure in the form "I slept happily," which,
by way of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), is rooted in both the experience and the experiencer; therefore, there must be an experiencer.

Because it is independent and self-luminous; for even in the state "I was unconscious of anything," the manifestation of emptiness (*śūnyaprakāśa*) still exists, since it must be admitted that in common worldly experience the aspect of the self’s own luminosity remains present, though devoid of its specific qualifiers.
Furthermore, because activities such as consciousness and so forth are impossible without resting in the supreme subject according to the direction shown, [the Lord]— by the aforementioned principle—
has encompassed within his own self-reflection the entire circle of existence and non-existence that has attained identity with his own Self.
The unification of the manifold powers such as knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance],
which takes the form of the experiencer, the rememberer, the conceptualizer,
and the recognizer, is autonomous, self-luminous, and consists of the vibration of the perfect "I" (pūrṇāhaṃ), whose nature is the synthesis of pure experience.
Because Maheśvara must be accepted [as the ultimate cause], the *avidyā-tattva*— which resides within the *puruṣa-tattva*— is regulated by the power of Maheśvara’s will (*icchā-śakti*) and,
through the door of *nivṛtti*, which consists in its abiding in a state of equilibrium with the power of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-śakti*) that serves as its own cause...
Aiming at the fruit characterized by one's own innate Śiva-nature, Brahman—
which is augmented by an undivided reflective awareness (amarśa) characterized by independent self-luminosity—
is the object; the desire to know it (*jijñāsā*)— by this term, "investigation" (*vicāra*) is indicated— is enjoined as that which ought to be performed.

The meaning is that one must perform the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) by way of non-difference from one's own Self, since the difference asserted by others has been refuted. In this aphorism, the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) summarizes the entire subject matter of the subsequent chapters on Concordance (*samanvaya*), Non-contradiction (*avirodha*), and Fruition (*phala*).

It should be understood through subtle insight that by the word *atha* (now/thereupon), the subject matter of the "Chapter on Means" (*sādhanādhyāya*) is summarized, and by the word *brahma*, the intended meaning is established as being of a nature characterized by self-luminosity and independence, which is distinct from both the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), and possesses inherent power (*śakti*).
Thus, by the mere contemplation of the meaning of this Sūtra, the person of the highest qualification certainly becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Now, what is the definition (lakṣaṇa) of that Brahman which has been thus indicated, without which [it cannot be known]?
Anticipating the objection that it is impossible to determine the true nature of the object, he says: "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this.

Of "this"—that is, of the phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of the moving and the unmoving, indicated by such examples as a jar or Caitra, which is perceived as something that can be pointed out with a finger.
"Birth and so forth"—birth (*janman*) means origination; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), maintenance, dissolution, bondage, and liberation are indicated.

That from which these arise—that is Brahman; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. And thus, there is the great proficiency in performing the fivefold cosmic acts known as creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace.

The intended meaning is that this is the unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman. In this regard, there are two [scriptural passages]: "That from which these beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they enter at their dissolution—desire to know that; that is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1), and "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).
The subject sentence means that those who are dying "enter" (abhisaṃviśanti) [Brahman];

the meaning is that having entered into Brahman, they attain identity with It. There is a doubt as to whether this definition is appropriate or not, because birth and so forth reside in the entire universe.

Because there is no connection with Brahman, because *sat*, *cit*, and *ānanda* are experienced in the world as having distinct meanings, and because of the difference in their verbal roots (*dhātu*),
it is impossible for them to constitute the nature of the indivisible Brahman; therefore, even these two definitions are not tenable.
The prima facie view.

To this it is replied: because the arising and destruction of a jar and so forth are impossible by themselves, as they are experienced as being dependent upon time and instruments; and because the instruments and so forth are dependent upon a limited subject through the medium of the organs of action and the rest; therefore, of that [subject]...

Since it cannot exist independently, being dependent on space, time, and other factors, the world resides in Brahman solely by virtue of being defined by Brahman; for this very reason, because of the existence of this relationship with Brahman, although "Being," "Consciousness," and "Bliss" have distinct meanings in common worldly usage, they possess a single uniform nature within Brahman. Not so.

It should not be argued that since the matter can be accomplished by a single term alone, why was it specified in three ways, as the employment of synonymous terms in a definition-sentence would be redundant;
for the word "existent" (*sat*) is used to highlight the distinction from non-existent entities such as a sky-flower, and [the word "consciousness"] is used to exclude even the insentient (*jaḍa*).

The word *cit* is recited there to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to that [Brahman] by virtue of its being of the nature of *sat* (existence); and the word *ānanda* (bliss) is recited to exclude over-extension to the individual soul (*jīva*), since the soul is of the nature of *sac-cit* (existence-consciousness).
This must be reflected upon, for since *cit* is to be accepted as "you are consciousness" (*cidasīti*), *sat* and *cit* are of one and the same form; therefore, it is *cit* alone [that is intended].
Since that which "rejoices" is also of the same nature as bliss, both definitions are indeed appropriate; such is the final conclusion (rāddhānta).
In this context, regarding the definition characterized by birth and so forth: the agency of creation alone is common to the four-faced Brahmā;
the agency of both creation and maintenance is common to Viṣṇu because he is the progenitor of the four-faced one;
and the agency of creation, maintenance, and destruction is common to Rudra because he is the progenitor of both of them.

According to the Śruti, "Dhātṛ is mine, Indra is mine, Viṣṇu is mine, and Indra is mine," the agency of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and concealment is common to the three forms (trimūrti) as they belong to the Lord;
however, [the Lord's] agency consists in creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace.

Because it is heard in scripture that [He] is "the Lord of Brahmā, the Lord of Brahman" as common to Sadāśiva, all four [deities] are subject to His control; therefore, it is stated that the defining characteristic is His great expertise in performing the five cosmic functions (*pañcakṛtya*).

Based on such scriptural passages as "The Self, verily, is space," since space and the person who identifies with it (puruṣa) arise from Brahman, Sadāśiva— who is the one identifying with space— is also included within the category of created beings and is therefore subject to the governance of Paraśiva.

Because of the absence of the great proficiency required for performing the five-fold cosmic acts, and because the agency over the universe is impossible for either the insentient or the individual soul (jīva), the definition of the essential nature known as Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda)— though not explicitly stated in the Sūtras— is made the intended subject matter.

Alternatively, there is the analysis: "From whom [comes] the birth and so forth of the first. This being established, it is supported by many scriptural passages, such as: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite"; "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman"; "The Supreme Brahman is Truth and Reality";
and "The Person, dark and tawny, with upraised semen and three eyes. Thus, according to the Śruti, [He is the source] of many.

Since Brahman has been established [as the subject], when the inquiry arises as to what the nature of that Brahman—designated as the object of desire to know—is, [the answer is: "Brahman is that from which the birth, or origin, of Nārāyaṇa occurs; he who was born prior to the first creation of the phenomenal world (prapañca), beginning with Brahmā and ending with the stationary objects. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, there arises a doubt as to whether this defining statement— "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed"— is untenable or tenable, since in the *Mahopaniṣad*, immediately following this sentence at the time of the commencement of creation,
it is heard: "Neither Brahmā nor Īśāna [existed]."

Because of the hearing of the negation of those two; and because of the hearing of their origin from Him alone, and because no other progenitor of them is heard of apart from Him— just like the scriptural passages establishing Brahman, such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"— prior to creation, there was only Nārāyaṇa alone.

Because of the hearing of its abiding [in all things], it is understood from this that the reality which is heard in all Vedāntas as the universal cause— generally described by terms such as "Being" (sat) and "Brahman"— is indeed Nārāyaṇa alone;
just as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice a beast to Agni and Soma," when there is doubt as to whether it is a cow or another animal, [the conclusion is] that it is a goat.
Regarding the phrase "from the color of the mantra," this refers to the well-known principle of the goat-sacrifice animal from the earlier Tantra;

for in this very context later on, in the section beginning with "Because of the inconsistency of the Lord," the author of the Sūtras himself refutes the possibility that Śiva is the cause of the universe. [Therefore,] the cause is Nārāyaṇa.
Indeed, this definition [of being "Brahman"] is untenable; on the contrary, because Brahman arises prior to the manifestation of Rudra and the rest,

Brahman alone is the primordial one, and because it is stated immediately after in scripture that "Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa" and "Rudra is born from Nārāyaṇa," therefore, of that which is primordial—

When it is argued that the definition—"Brahman is that from which the birth of Brahman occurs"—applies only to Nārāyaṇa, we reply: in the *Atharvaśikhā*, this is in accordance with the questions introduced at the beginning, namely, "What is that meditation? Who is the meditator? And what is the object of meditation?"

Since it is stated in scripture that "Viṣṇu is meditation (dhyāna), Rudra is the meditator (dhyātā), and one should meditate upon Īśāna as the object of meditation," there is here a contradiction between Rudra— who is included among those prohibited in the Nārāyaṇa-tantra well-known in the Mahopaniṣad— and [the aforementioned scriptural statement].

Having described the nature of meditation and the meditator through the relationship of degrees of intensity (*taratamabhāva*), it is subsequently understood that there exists no Maheśāna superior to Nārāyaṇa, because Īśāna is prescribed as the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). Now, regarding Īśāna...

In order to dispel the doubt as to how that [Brahman] can be an object of meditation given the hearing of its negation, the following is stated immediately after: "All this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the sense organs along with the elements—is produced from Him; He is not a cause, for He is the Cause."

It is heard here that "He is to be meditated upon" (dhyeya), due to the inherent force of that word; and because of the root *īś* meaning "supreme sovereignty," [this refers] to the Supreme Lord Sadāśiva, who is synonymous with Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa, as distinguished from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra mentioned in the *Mahopaniṣad*, and from the other well-known *Īśvara* indicated by the term "Indra."
And by the statement regarding "being born together" (*saṃprasūti*) with the elements and sense organs that have become insentient,

and because it is understood from that that [the individual soul] arises as something dependent on that same [cause], it is indicated by the phrase "is not the cause" that Īśāna, who is the cause of this, is not born.

Regarding the phrase "But the cause, however, is to be meditated upon" (*kāraṇaṃ tu dhyeyaḥ*): because of the natural force of the word "but" (*tu*) here, and because of the hearing of a prohibition against Īśāna who has entered the category of effects, it is indicated that the Īśāna who is the cause is the one to be meditated upon.
Here, in order to dispel the doubt that—since it is stated "the cause, however, is to be meditated upon"—that cause might be something else entirely, [the text proceeds].

The meaning is that He is the *dhātṛ*, the protector, of the causes—the five Brahmās beginning with Brahmā—who are regulated in their functions such as creation as previously described; or, He is the *dhyātṛ*, one who delights in His own Self, or the original agent of volition; and here He is endowed with all sovereignty and is the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*).

By the force of the word *cakāra* (and), the meaning is that he is denoted by the term "Lord of All" (*sarveśvara*). *Śambhu* means that Śiva alone is to be meditated upon in the midst of space; he is the maker of auspiciousness and the bestower of liberation. And the fruit of meditation has been stated:
having abandoned everything else—other deities who are afflicted by birth and death—[one should meditate on him].

The meaning is "having abandoned. Because it is clearly heard [in the text] that the *Atharvaśikhā* has reached its conclusion, with the intention that there is no further portion to be stated beyond this, it declares its own completion by itself.

From the understanding that "Śiva alone is to be meditated upon," which refers even to Nārāyaṇa—the cause of the universe consisting of Brahmā and others—as established in the Mahopaniṣad, [it follows that Śiva is the ultimate cause]; for in the passage "Verily, Nārāyaṇa was alone," the word "was" (āsīt) implies: "Rohita arose from the red [Nārāyaṇa]," and "Parāśara arose from Śakti."
Thus, because the focus on the existence of his birth is necessarily present, the definition is indeed appropriate. Now, one might object:
"In this context, neither the birth of Nārāyaṇa nor his superiority relative to the meditating Rudra is heard;
rather, it is Viṣṇu alone [who is meant], since there exist infinite incarnations of Viṣṇu, who is Nārāyaṇa."
