If it is argued that because [Nārāyaṇa] is the form of their descent, or because—as established by the Gītā statement "Among the Ādityas, I am Viṣṇu"—he is a portion (*aṃśin*) of them, it is logical that he is the primary referent; and therefore, it is appropriate that the words "Īśāna" and so forth used here refer to Nārāyaṇa through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), we say: no.

Since it is impossible for the word "Viṣṇu," which is recited in the midst of the primary [deities] Brahmā and Rudra, to refer merely to an incarnation or a partial manifestation (avatārāṃśa), one must understand it as such according to the maxim of the *Pūrvatantravārtika*: "Whatever is heard predominantly, that is how it is understood. Otherwise, what would be the cause for [the text] stating "Brahman is the cause"?

Since those who discourse on Brahman and are in doubt are unable to reach a conclusion by themselves, when they meditate upon the Goddess and, through her grace, conclude that Śiva alone is Brahman— the cause of the universe— as stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "When..."

There is neither darkness nor day, neither night nor existence, nor non-existence; Śiva alone is absolute. Out of fear, some take refuge in Him who is unborn, O Rudra—protect me eternally with that face of Yours which is turned to the south.
When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, then...

Having established— on the basis of the scriptural statement that "the cessation of suffering will occur through not knowing Śiva"— that at the time prior to creation, when only the darkness (*tamas*) characterized by ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is synonymous with *prakṛti* and serves as the material cause of the universe, remained,
there was an absence of the distinction between existence and non-existence characterized as day and night; [he proceeds as follows].
Because, by hearing of the very state of Sadāśiva, the existence of a second [entity] is impossible; because he is heard to be unborn;
and because he is heard to be the object of prayer for those seeking liberation who are tormented by birth and death.

Furthermore, because scripture declares that the knowledge of Śiva alone bestows liberation, and because it is impossible for that [knowledge] to have origination or destruction, the various forms of Rudra who are his incarnations— such as those mentioned in the Śruti passage beginning "The thousands upon thousands of Rudras who are on the earth"—
possess that same nature; thus, even their origination and destruction therein are merely apparent.

The two [entities] must be none other than Īśāna and Parā, because it is impossible for both to exist prior to creation; furthermore, this is supported by the force of the qualification "bṛhat" (the Great) in another Vedic passage: "Thus Viṣṇu, the knower of the Supreme, from which the Brahman protects the triad."

It is understood that Mahāviṣṇu alone possesses the quality of being subject to origination, the state of being a knower of the Supreme Self, and the role of protector of the royal capital of Paraśiva— which consists of the pure phenomenal world (prapañca) that is distinct from the impure and the mixed; this is according to the direction shown for the word "was" (āsīt) in that context.
Since the existence of [Śiva] as something produced is necessarily excluded,
and because the conceptualization of him through various terms such as Śiva and Śambhu lacks scriptural authority,
[the scripture] speaks of the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, three-eyed and blue-throated, in the context of the revelation of liberation (kaivalya-śruti).

Having meditated upon that which is profoundly peaceful, the sage goes to the source of all beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness. He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra; he is the imperishable, supreme self-ruler.
He alone is Viṣṇu, he is Prāṇa, he is Time, Fire, and the Moon. Whatever has been and whatever is yet to be—[all that is he].

Having spoken thus, and having known Him, one transcends death; there is no other path to liberation. Because this is heard in the Śruti as a negation of other paths, and because the Supreme Lord—who is to be meditated upon by those seeking liberation—is described as being accompanied by Umā, as having three eyes, and as having a blue throat, these [attributes]...
Furthermore, because Śiva constitutes only a single portion [of the whole], it is in no way possible for him to be the supreme Nārāyaṇa.

This being the case, in the section beginning with "Because of the inconsistency of the Lord" (*patyurasāmañjasyāt*), [the Lord] was refuted on account of His being accepted by the Tantric Pāśupatas as the sole efficient cause of the universe.
For this very reason, in the section beginning with "He is known from the word alone" (*śabdādeva pramitaḥ*), [it is stated that] the person is thumb-sized and situated in the middle...

Regarding the mantra from the Kaṭhavallī, "The Lord dwells within the self, the master of what has been and what is to be; He alone is the one of today and the one of tomorrow," one might suspect that it refers to the individual soul (jīva) because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of having a limited dimension;
however, this is refuted by the use of the particle *eva* ("alone"), even though the qualifying term "of what has been and what is to be" is present.

This is because, having set aside the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the lordship over past and future entities, it has been accepted that the word "Īśāna" (Lord) refers to Brahman on account of its verbal form and other factors.

Furthermore, in this section concerning the inclusion of the moving and the unmoving (*carācaragrahaṇāt*), there is a doubt raised regarding the mantra found in the second Vallī of the Kaṭhaka Upaniṣad: "He for whom both Brahmin and Kṣatriya are food, and for whom death is the condiment—who knows that? Having raised the suspicion that this mantra refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the digestive fire (*agni*), [the author] refutes it on the grounds that both of these are themselves seized by death.
Since it has been stated that "death is its condiment," it is understood that [the subject] is the agent of the dissolution of the phenomenal world of moving and non-moving beings;

and since this mantra has been determined to refer to the Lord (Īśvara) and it is accepted that being the destroyer of the universe is a defining characteristic of the Lord, Śiva is the agent of dissolution.
Because this is well-established, it follows that such a Lord Paśupati cannot possibly be the sole efficient cause of the universe by virtue of his acceptance of the Pāśupata doctrine,
due to the resulting inconsistency; he would be like a potter and others, who depend upon other material causes such as clay that are distinct from themselves.

Because, through the dissolution of orientation toward one's own self and the resulting orientation toward something else, there would arise a dependence on unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, which would entail the consequence of a lack of sovereignty; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Because the Śruti declares, "Rudra is the great seer (maharṣi) superior to all," his status as superior to the universe is heard;
and because he is a seer of all mantras, whereas others are seers of only individual mantras, he is a great seer.
For this very reason, due to his being the highest among Brāhmaṇas, he is to be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas, even [in receiving] the water used for washing his feet and his grace.

The two [Śiva and Viṣṇu] are to be accepted [as liberated], because they are the objects of the grace of the Guṇirudra-tīrtha situated within the universe resulting from the curses of Bhṛgu and others;

because it is possible for Bhṛgu and the others to have maintained such a contemplation until that point; and because it is a place of liberation (muktasthāna). "Not he" (na sa)—[refers to the one who has not attained this].

Because of the Vedic revelation, "He returns again," let this digression suffice. Since the Veda declares, "The universe is Nārāyaṇa, Hari," and because the *Sahasranāma* (Thousand Names) records, "Viṣṇu is the universe, he is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance," Viṣṇu is contained within the universe. Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "the Lord of the universe," he possesses the status of being the Lord of the universe. Of him...

There is no contradiction because [the term "para"] is used with reference to the universe in its form as his own effect; for in the passage "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman," it is logical that Nārāyaṇa is the Brahman who is beyond [all else], whereas in other places where the reading is "Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman" (nārāyaṇaḥ paraṃ brahma),

The Veda must have a creator, because it is understood to arise without effort according to the analogy of "breathing forth" (*niśvasita-nyāya*);
