The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) here is as follows: because [the Veda] is composed of sentences by Kalidasa and others—which, though produced without conscious effort according to the analogy of breathing, convey meaning—it differs [from the Veda]; furthermore, since it arises at each creation identical to its predecessor, it is impossible for it to be eternal in the form of a continuous stream (*pravāha*). Thus, it lacks the status of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*).

By defining Brahman as the author of the Veda, which illuminates the arrangement of the entire universe, its omniscience is established. It should be understood that its status as the creator of all was already defined in the preceding sūtra. Alternatively, one might ask: what [is the purpose] regarding Brahman characterized by such definitions?
In response to the inquiry as to what constitutes the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he says: "Because it has the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).

In this regard, the scriptural passage stating, "I create that person who is rooted in the Upaniṣads" (*taṃ caupaniṣadaṃ puruṣaṃ sṛjāmi*)—which is an alternative reading for *tatra tatraikaṃ tvaupaniṣadam*—is the subject matter. Here, the question arises whether Brahman is accessible through means of valid knowledge such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, or not.
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that because it is an established entity like a jar or other objects, it must be cognizable through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). [To this we reply:

Due to the absence of form, taste, and so forth, it lacks suitability for the sense organs; nor is it within the range of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because that would entail its being insentient (*jaḍatva*), like pleasure, pain, and the like. Furthermore, [the claim that] pleasure and so forth [are modifications of] the internal organ—
It might be argued that insentience is logical because [objects] are knowable by consciousness delimited [by adjuncts],
whereas the Self is not insentient because it is the object of the internal organ alone;
however, this is said precisely with the intention that, since the internal organ is insentient, its capacity to be a knower is impossible.

It is accepted that pleasure in a jar and the like are cognizable by consciousness delimited by a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Likewise, in the present case as well, since the internal organ— being insentient— is incapable of being a cognizer,
it must be accepted that [the object] is cognizable by consciousness delimited by its modification.
Because the consequence of insentience would be unavoidable, inference is also not [the means of knowledge],
since it is rooted in perception and thus lacks the capacity to reveal the Great Lord as something entirely unlimited; otherwise,
by appearing as included within that [perception], He would fall into the predicament of being limited.

Because it is impossible for something to be manifested by that [consciousness] while not being included within it, it must be external to it. If it is argued that this is possible—just as space is inferred through the mark (liṅga) of sound—we reply that space, too, is limited because it is produced; since it is an object of that [manifestation], it must be of the same nature as it. Otherwise, it would be like water and other such things.
Because it would follow that [the object] possesses the nature of each respective [limited attribute], and because inference— being restricted to specific particulars—
cannot possibly have Brahman as its essential nature; likewise, even the status of being an object of verbal knowledge is impossible,
due to [Brahman's] being limited and being cognizable by a consciousness other than itself.

If it is argued that [the Self] would otherwise result in being insentient like a jar or similar objects, and that the Śruti states, "By what means could one know the Knower who is without support?", then this must be considered as follows:
since the Veda is understood to be of the nature of the effortless exhalation (*niśvasita*) of the Great Lord (*Īśvara*), whoever...

According to the Vedic revelation, "He who indeed creates Brahmā first and imparts the Vedas to him," it is stated that the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the teacher of the network of words that are the Vedas to Brahmā; for this [teaching] is dependent upon His will, which is His volition (*icchā*).

Because it possesses objects, there are four measured quarters of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them: "Three, hidden in the cave, they do not set in motion; of speech, mortals speak only the fourth"—so says the Śruti.

This is because one realizes that [the object] possesses the nature of self-reflection (*svavimarśa*) through the forms of *ārambha*, *vivakṣā*, *adhyavasāya*, and *ukti*— which are synonyms for *vaikhary-ādi*— characterized by the stages of sprouting, having sprouted, budding, and bearing fruit; therefore, it is not distinct from itself.

Because it is capable of revealing the majesty of that [Brahman] which has not been previously attained by anything else, the established conclusion is that Brahman is the great sovereignty accessible only through the Veda as the sole means of valid cognition.

And thus, the meaning of the Sūtra is that [the Lord] is the source (*yoni*) of the scripture—that is, of the means of valid cognition consisting of the words of the Vedas, Āgamas, and so forth—because He possesses the capacity to manifest its majesty. Now, an objection is raised: it is not possible for the Upaniṣads to have Brahman as their primary purport, because they would otherwise be purposeless, serving only the utility of ritual performance.

If [the Upanishads] were devoted solely to the means of accomplishing the agent and the deity, they would have purpose only as being useful for ritual performance; however, since the expansion of the definition of the meaning of words is of a nature different from consciousness (cit),
it is impossible for it to have Brahman as its material cause, and thus the aforementioned definition [of the Upanishads] is untenable— anticipating this objection, he says:

"But that [Brahman is the cause], because of the coordination [of all things with it]. The word "but" (*tu*) serves to refute the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Here, the subject passage (*viṣayavākya*) begins with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" and ends with "That is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu. Are the Vedāntas devoted to ritual action (*karma*), or...?

There is a doubt as to whether [the means] is the Brahman; for regarding heaven— defined as pleasure unadulterated by the obstacles of suffering— the Vedic injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" enjoin ritual action alone.
Precisely by virtue of the *apūrva* residing in the sacrificer produced by that [action], the production of the constituent elements serving as its means occurs,

and heaven— which arises in another body at another time— is possible. And thus, among the Vedāntas, those passages that set forth the individual soul (*jīva*) refer to the agent-sacrificer, while those passages that set forth Brahman...

If it is accepted that [the Vedas] are devoted to the deities—that is, that sentences teaching creation are devoted to means such as substances—then the Vedāntas would have purposefulness by virtue of being useful for ritual performance; however, if they were devoted to Brahman, their purposefulness would be absent, resulting in futility. Therefore, they are subordinate to ritual action by being devoted to the agent, the deity, and the means.
When it has thus been reached that they are not intent upon Brahman, we reply:
Because the Vedāntas are studied within distinct contexts, it is impossible for them to be subordinate to ritual action (*karma*);

for they possess the six marks that determine the intended meaning (*tātparya-nirṇaya*), namely: the opening and concluding statements, repetition, novelty, result, explanatory praise, and consistency—thereby having Brahman as their ultimate purport.
For instance, the opening statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and the concluding statement, "All this has that as its self;
that is the Truth; that is the Self; thou art That"—these two share the single characteristic of having Brahman as their subject matter.
The repetition "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) constitutes the practice (*abhyāsa*).

Its novelty (*apūrvatva*) consists in the great sovereignty that is not accessible through other means of knowledge. Its fruit is the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one, expressed in such passages as: "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known."
Just as when clay is known, its effects such as jars and bowls are understood to be non-different from it because they are its products— such is the meaning;
the five explanatory doctrines (arthavādas) consist of creation, maintenance, dissolution, entry, and restriction.
The examples of clay and so forth are logical justifications because, by these marks, [the texts] have Brahman as their ultimate purport.

Nor is there an absence of purpose without practice, since there is the possibility of the great fruit consisting in the emergence of the full sense of "I" (pūrṇāhaṃbhāva) through the submergence of the egoity (ahaṃtā) regarding the body and other such things. Now, if this is so...
Even though the Vedāntas have Brahman as their ultimate purport, they do not terminate in Brahman alone;

rather, having first established the reality of Brahman through the indirect method in the passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," they subsequently bring about its direct realization. This being the case, because the Vedāntas provide instruction [in this manner],...

The status of being a *śāstra* (authoritative scripture) is established because it conveys a meaning not previously understood. However, after enjoining "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*), which consists of verbal knowledge, there subsequently follow the injunctions "it is to be reflected upon" (*maṃtavya*) and "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*), which consist of experiential knowledge. Therefore, the Vedāntas—

If it is argued that [the Upanishads] are prescriptive of practice (*pratipatti*), we say no; because they cannot be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise, they lack the nature of a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*), and thus a prescription for practice is simply not possible. Furthermore, there is no fixed rule that the status of being a scripture (*śāstratva*) belongs only to that which teaches what is to be accomplished (*anuṣṭheya-śāsana*), for that status is established even by means of proving an already existing reality (*siddha-vastu*). Therefore, it is not so.

And it is not reasonable to say that after the object is known through verbal cognition, reflection (*manana*) and so forth— which are of the nature of direct experience— are subsequently enjoined; for, as in the case of "You are the tenth," the word itself generates immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*), and thus [the practice] must occur prior to the verbal comprehension.
Because the injunctions regarding reflection (*manana*) and so forth— which consist of the activity of an agent— are intended to eliminate [doubts] such as the impossibility [of liberation],

and because the sole purpose of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the removal of delusion, as is experienced in cases such as "this jar is here because it is perceptible," [it follows that] in this context, the jar is not being produced.

Because it is already established, it is not made known [by inference]; rather, since it is known by perception itself, the delusion that it is "non-pointed" is removed by the proof that it is "pointed. Similarly, the delusion regarding the nature of possessing fire is dispelled by proving the possession of fire through the mark of smoke; thus, the Vedāntas [teach] only with respect to Brahman.
This is established because of the scriptural statement, "All this has that as its self; that is the Truth";

for in all cases, including universals and the like, existence (*sattā*) is observed to persist in the form of "the jar exists," "the cloth exists," and so forth, as a persistence of an essential existence (*svarūpasattā*) that is distinct from insentient matter.

Because the effect pre-exists [in the cause], that which has been stated as the definition [of the Self] is also logically established; for it is impossible for an insentient entity to maintain its existence through its own power, as that would entail independence,
and the manner in which it is impossible for it to maintain its existence through the power of another has already been demonstrated.

The nature of pure consciousness (sacciddhanatva) must be accepted even against one's will; for action, being insentient, lacks the effort to produce the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), and the unseen merit, likewise being insentient,
lacks the effort to produce heaven or the substances that serve as its means.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that Brahman alone— which is independent, self-luminous, and the very essence of the existence of all phenomenal manifestation— is what is propounded by all the Vedāntas. This being so, because the Vedāntas possess a coherent harmony (*samanvaya*) with respect to Brahman through the six marks that determine their intended meaning (*tātparya*), [Brahman is the sole reality].
The meaning is that Brahman possesses great sovereignty, being accessible through the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) characterized as previously stated.
Now, an objection may be raised: since the Śruti declares, "For this Puruṣa is indeed unattached," it is impossible for Brahman to be the cause of the universe;
rather, the causal statements in the Vedāntas refer only to the Pradhāna. Thus...

Anticipating the objection that [the Pradhāna] is heard [in scripture], he says: "Because of seeing (īkṣateḥ), it is not 'non-scriptural' (aśabdam). The analysis of the compound is: "not non-scriptural because of seeing. In the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, having introduced [the topic] with, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second—Brahman," it continues: "It thought (aikṣata): May I be many..."
"It thought, 'May I be many,' and it created fire"—thus it is heard in scripture. This is the subject passage (*viṣayavākya*).
Here, a doubt arises as to whether that which is denoted by the word "it" (*tat*) is the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), the cause of the universe, or Brahman.
On this point, the Sāṃkhyas say: that which is denoted by the word "it," the cause of the entire world, is indeed the *pradhāna*.

Because it is heard in scripture that "there is one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form," and because she is endowed with the quality of *sattva* and possesses the inherent nature of transformation,
the powers of knowledge and action are also possible for her; whereas Brahman, being devoid of distinctions...

To the objection that [Brahman cannot be the cause] because of the impossibility of that [reflection], we reply: since the quality of being a seer is heard in the passage "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), and since that is impossible for the Pradhāna due to its insentience, that which is denoted by the word "That" is indeed the conscious Brahman;
moreover, it possesses both freedom from attachment and the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*).

Because [the self] is devoid of qualities distinct from itself as accepted by the Naiyāyikas, it must be admitted that knowledge and action are not distinct from its own nature; otherwise, the consequence of insentience (jaḍatva) would follow. If this were accepted, it would be impossible for the Puruṣa to be the impeller of Prakṛti.

The production of the universe would not even be possible, because, due to the insentience (*jaḍatva*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), it lacks the capacity to produce effects without a prompter. Nor can it be argued that a figurative act of seeing (*gauṇam īkṣaṇam*) is possible for the Pradhāna—as in the case of [the statement] "fire and water saw"—for [the text continues]: "Come, let me enter these three deities with this... and so forth.
"Having entered by means of the living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms"— in this intermediate statement,
the deity who is the cause of the universe, the evolver of names and forms which have not yet been abandoned,
designates the conscious individual soul (jīva) by the word "self" (ātman) as its own designator; thus, in the conclusion, [the text says] "That is the Self."
In the statement "That thou art, O Śvetaketu," the identity with the cause of the world is taught by the Guru to the disciple; thus, even a figurative seeing is impossible here.
Now, one might object that in this context, it is heard in scripture: "Having entered with the living self (jīva-ātman), let me evolve names and forms."

Because the individual soul (jīva) is understood to be the cause of the universe, one might ask: "How can being the cause of the universe be an exclusive characteristic of Brahman? To this we reply: no, because the word *jīva* refers to a conscious entity whose nature consists of knowledge and action; for one who is a *jīva*, there must be knowing and acting.

"By the supreme yogi: the presence or absence of vision and action are the causes of sovereignty and insentience. Because this is stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, and because it is impossible to explain the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) without knowledge and action;
[one might object]: "Even so, however, having knowledge and action as one's essential nature is common to all individual souls (*jīva*)."
If it is argued that the very principle of the Puruṣa (Spirit) might be what is denoted by that word [“Brahman”], we say no;
for even the Self is not the master over the cause of pleasure and pain, since scripture declares, “Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—
they too are brought forth,” and because Brahmā and the others are equal to the elements, the senses, and so forth.

Because it is impossible for [the self] to be the cause of the universe— given that it is heard to arise dependent on another and is afflicted by pleasure, pain, and so forth— and because it is included within the category of effects, the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) who is its cause is one endowed with all sovereignty and is the Lord of All (*sarveśvara*).

Because of the scriptural revelation of [Brahman's] possession of all sovereignty and its being denoted by the term "Lord of All," and because of the instruction for liberation—namely, "That is the Self; thou art That"—concerning the Puruṣa residing in Prakṛti, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. Furthermore, since it is observed that scorpions and other creatures arise from cow-dung and similar substances...

Furthermore, from the analogy of the spider (*ūrṇanābhi*), because Brahman is independent, it does not depend upon any other auxiliary cause distinct from itself. Otherwise, being devoid of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*),
Brahman would fall into unreality (*alīkatva*), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
The established conclusion is that Brahman itself, augmented by the power of self-dependent self-luminosity, is what is denoted by that word.

And thus, the Pradhāna—being devoid of sound and lacking the capacity for speech—cannot be the cause of the universe; for the Sūtra states "because of seeing," meaning because of the scriptural hearing of its being a seer. In this section, the entire subject matter of the subsequent chapter on "Non-contradiction" (Avirodha) is summarized.

Because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon that [Brahman], the meaning of the entire *Sādhanādhyāya* is subsumed within the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*, the meaning of the *Samanvayādhyāya* within the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, and the meaning of the *Phalādhyāya* within the *Utsūtra* (the statement following the *Samanvaya-sūtra*). Thus, for a person of the highest qualification, the Brahma-vidyā extends only up to the word "Iksati" (It is seen).

It should be understood that the *Pañcapādikā* was intended for the intermediate qualified seeker (*madhyamādhikārī*), whereas the *Avaśiṣṭa-śāstra* was composed for the inferior qualified seeker (*adhamādhikārī*). Herein [is discussed] the nature of the Self as Being (*sadrūpa*), which is common to all and constitutes the essence of the meaning of the *praṇava*; its superiority over the insentient (*jaḍa*); and its distinction from the individual soul (*jīva*).

It should be observed with a subtle vision that only the definition of one's own true nature— known as form, existence, consciousness, and bliss, and endowed with the great sovereignty of the moment— has been made manifest.

In the beginning, there is non-difference [of the effect] from that [cause], on account of the words concerning "originating" (ārambhaṇa) and so forth. [Objection: If [the cause] undergoes modification (pariṇāma) by making itself [the effect], there would either be the consequence of the entire [cause] being exhausted, or else a contradiction with the scriptural texts stating that [Brahman] is partless. [Reply: This is not so, because [the cause] acts upon itself, and indeed [the world] is manifold within it.
But it is mere illusion, because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety; for the other [the individual soul] is not possible [in this context].

By such sūtras as these, the fact that the creator of the insentient and sentient universe is non-different from Maheśvara is specifically revealed; here, by the word "māyā," the innate primordial nature (prakṛti) is denoted, according to the Śruti: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā."

And by the etymological derivation "she who possesses an excellent form" (*prakṛṣṭākṛti*), this very power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which is the nature of the agent and is most capable of accomplishing the impossible, is called *vidyā*. Therefore, there is no contradiction in saying that this very [power] is *avidyā*— meaning it is not [true] knowledge (*vidyā*) because it is false (*mithyābhūta*)— since [the term *avidyā*] consists of its constituent parts [as *na-vidyā*].

Because of the subsequent statement, "This world of mobile and immobile beings is pervaded [by Him]," and because it is understood that the entire universe is pervaded by Nārāyaṇa— who exists as a limb or partial incarnation of Maheśvara, the master of Māyā— it is said: "The organ of hearing and the object of hearing are Nārāyaṇa."

And from such scriptural passages as these, it should be understood that Nārāyaṇa alone is the material cause of the future universe in relation to [the primordial state], and thus his nature consists of the aspect of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).
I am the taste in the waters, O son of Kuntī; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun;
I am the syllable Om in all the Vedas; I am the sound in space, and the virility in men.

And because it has been sung thus: "This being the case, since Brahman possesses consciousness by virtue of its nature as vision and action, and since Śiva has likewise aphorized that 'consciousness is the Self,' there is no contradiction between the *Brahma-sūtra* and the *Śiva-sūtra*, as they both rest upon the same single meaning. Thus, there is unity of the scriptures (*śāstraikya*)."
This is to be investigated.

Now, by the word "vi," knowledge that brings about the realization of the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) is expressed. Those Śaivas who delight in that [knowledge] are proclaimed as Vīraśaivas; for there is no contradiction with this statement from their own established doctrine (siddhānta), their unity should therefore be reflected upon. Such is the tenet of that [school].

Because it establishes the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*, for instance, in their scriptures: "The dense *liṅga* is of great luster, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss; it is partless, actionless, tranquil, independent, and self-luminous. This is because it serves as the locus for all things and likewise as their place of dissolution."

The ground of the principles beginning with Mahat is called *sthala*. That *sthala* is known as the Brahman in which the phenomenal world dissolves—the infinite, immovable support, whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss. By the mere agitation of its own power, that *sthala* is twofold.
One is declared to be the *liṅgasthala* (the station of the *liṅga*), and the other is remembered as the *aṅgasthala* (the station of the limbs).

The *liṅgasthala* is to be known as threefold, according to the distinctions of *bhāva*, *prāṇa*, and *iṣṭa*. The first would be the *bhāvaliṅga*, the second the *prāṇaliṅga*, and the third the *iṣṭaliṅga*; thus it is threefold.
It is taught that each single site is further twofold, and each of those two types is again twofold.

The Śivaliṅga is divided into the Mahāliṅga, the one called Prasāda, and that which arises from the classification of the Bhāvaliṅga; furthermore, it is distinguished as the Jaṅgama, born from the Prāṇaliṅga. Likewise, the Guruliṅga and the Ācāraliṅga are distinguished according to their respective desired divisions.

Thus has the "limb-region" (aṅgasthala) been described by the teachers who perceive with subtle vision. The first is declared to be the limb of yoga (yogāṅga), the second the limb of enjoyment (bhogāṅga), and the third the limb of renunciation (tyāgāṅga);
thus it is remembered as being threefold. The limb of yoga is oneness and taking refuge.

The two [stages] known as *sthala* (the station) constitute both [aspects]. The pair consisting of *prāṇaliṅgin* (one whose liṅga is the vital breath) and *prasādī* (one who has received grace) is intended as the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*). The two stations known as *māheśvara-sthala* (the station of the Great Lord) and *bhakta-sthala* (the station of the devotee) are declared by the seers of reality to be the limbs of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*). Such is the meaning.
The reality that serves as the foundational locus for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire phenomenal world is designated by the word "sthala."

That reality, whose sole form is the manifestation of the primordial *praṇava* characterized as previously described, is the supreme Śiva-principle; it is self-luminous because it appears independently of any other means of knowledge,
and it is self-acting because it functions without dependence on any other cause.

Independent, and for that very reason existing without dependence on anything else; and for that very reason consisting of the manifestation of existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), characterized by objectless, non-sequential self-awareness— in such a Supreme Śiva, whose nature is the perfect I-consciousness, within the play of the worshipped and the worshipper—
Just as a wave arises in a waveless ocean, a slight movement first arises within its own self;
by that movement, there occurs a mere portion of independent self-luminosity in which [the subject and object] have become mutually blended in a single essence.
Due to the mere absence of supreme agency, it is divided into two types according to its inferior or superior state.

Among these, when there is self-luminosity characterized by a superior state, the very consciousness of Śiva— in the form of the primordial *praṇava* which has entered through the process of radiance— becomes the *liṅga-tattva*.
When its own self-luminosity has been diminished, the very consciousness of Śiva that has entered therein becomes the *aṅga-tattva*. In that state, however, the *liṅga-tattva* [arises] gradually.

The *bhāvaliṅga*—which consists of the movement of the reflection of *saccidānanda* (Being-Consciousness-Bliss)—is threefold: it is the *prāṇaliṅga*, the *iṣṭaliṅga*, and the *prasādaliṅga*. Furthermore, each of these three *liṅgas* is twofold. Among them, the *bhāvaliṅga* is indeed the *mahāliṅga* and the *prasādaliṅga*.
The *prāṇaliṅga* is of two kinds: the *jaṅgamaliṅga* and the *śivaliṅga*. The *iṣṭaliṅga* is of two kinds: the *guruliṅga* and the *ācāraliṅga*.
Thus, the category of *liṅgas* is sixfold.

That very power of autonomous self-luminosity, within these signs (*liṅga*) such as *krama*, is the *kalā* known as *uttarā*, which transcends *śānti*; it is the synonym for the *cit-śakti* that serves as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) for the subtle manifestation of the world of effects and instruments, and whose form is the *praṇava*.
The Kalā of Śāntyatīta, consisting of the syllable *ya*, which is another synonym for the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*) whose nature is bliss;
the Kalā of Śānti, consisting of the syllable *vā*, which is another synonym for the Power of Direction (*ādi-śakti*) characterized by the orientation toward manifestation (*unmukhya*);
and the Kalā of Vidyā, consisting of the syllable *śi*, which is another synonym for the Power of Will (*icchā-śakti*) characterized by subtle activity (*sūkṣma-kriyā*).

Thus, it attained a sixfold nature: first, as the *pratiṣṭhākalā*, consisting of the letter A, which is another name for the outward-turned power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*); and second, as the *nivṛttikalā*, consisting of the letter Na, which is another name for the gross power of action (*kriyāśakti*) characterized by exertion. And in this way, it became the Great Liṅga.
Because its nature is the heart characterized by the continuous contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of all categories of existence,
it is called the "hidden face" (*gopyamukha*), which is the form of the pure contemplator. As for the five signs (*liṅga*) beginning with serenity (*prasāda*),
they [arise] in succession.

It is called the "manifest five faces"— namely Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta— which consist of the forms that contemplate specific objects such as sound and so forth. Thus, for this principle of Liṅga-tattva,
there is a pure contemplation characterized by a predominance of differentiation that culminates in non-differentiation, according to the analogy of the waves of the ocean.
It is called "the object of worship" (upāsya) because it is the cause of grace by virtue of being the nature of the *mātṛkā*. Thus, the reality of the limbs (*aṅgatattva*) is threefold:
the limb of yoga characterized by the contemplation of the union of identity among one's own self, the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama*.
The limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) is characterized by the transformation into the bliss of accepting that which is most worthy of being taken up as a favor bestowed by Him;
the limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*) consists of the non-deceptive abandonment of body, mind, and wealth toward the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama*.
Furthermore, each of these is of two kinds. The limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*), however, is oneness (*aikya*) and seeking refuge (*śaraṇa*).

It is divided. The limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*) is divided into *prāṇaliṅgin* and *prasādin*. The limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*) is divided into *māheśvara* and *bhaktasthala*. Thus, there are six kinds of illuminations of the limbs.
That very power, having attained a state of diminution,

assumes the form of sixfold devotion: namely, devotion as the state of equal flavor (*samarasa*), devotion as bliss (*ānanda*), devotion as experience (*anubhava*), devotion as attentiveness (*avadhāna*), devotion as steadfastness (*naiṣṭhika*), and devotion as faith (*śraddhā*).
It assumes the state of the sixfold internal organ characterized by the objective world, cognition, mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness;

it takes on the form of the six sense organs of knowledge beginning with the ear; and it manifests as the six categories characterized by satisfaction regarding their respective objects, such as sound and the rest.
The state of being the six-syllabled mantra that expresses it;
the state of being the organs of action, such as speech and the rest, which serve as the means for ritual action;
and the state of being the collective totality of the five subtle elements, beginning with ether.
And having attained the state of being the sixfold form known as Sadbhāva, Sujñāna, Sumanas, Nirahaṃkāra, Subuddhi, and Sucitta,
it became an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*).
Although such an auxiliary reality (*aṅgatattva*) possesses a nature consisting of contracted powers of consciousness and so forth, as fashioned by the playful power (*līlā-śakti*) of Maheśvara.

Because it is conjoined with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as subtle form, the mental organ, and space, and because its nature consists primarily of differentiation based on the divisions of the upward-emanated creation, it is called the "worshipper" (*upāsaka*), being of the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*).
And thus, the principle of the *liṅga* is a limb of the principle of *śaraṇa*, and the *liṅga* of *śaraṇa* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Between these two, there is indeed a state of mutual identity, according to the analogy of the seed and the tree. Thus, from time immemorial, the *liṅga* is the refuge and the refuge is the *liṅga*; this is certainly so. Now, because such a refuge possesses the recognition of one's own Self (*svātmapratyabhijñāna*), which is attained through the glance of the Guru characterized by self-reflection (*svavimarśa*), [it is established].

This very mind is the great liṅga in the form of the Praṇava; because it is inward-turned, it serves as the means for grasping all objects— sound and the rest— which are the respective domains of each of the external senses characterized by the ear and so forth.

Because it is the cause of grace (*anugraha*) through the sequence beginning with *paśyantī*— consisting of the utterance of the resolve, the scriptures, and the words of the Teacher whose form is the Great Sound (*mahānāda*), the Sound (*nāda*), and the Resounding Sound (*sunāda*)— the very organ of hearing (*śrotra*), which is the means for perceiving sound,
is the sign of grace in the form of the letter *ya*; for "moving" (*cara*) and "stationary" (*jaṅgama*) are synonyms, and its [the ear's] skin...
Pervading all limbs, it is the means for experiencing sensations such as cold and so forth;

thus, the mobile *liṅga* consisting of the syllable *Vā* is indeed the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*) itself. Having entered the eyeball, because it is the means for illuminating all objects of form, the eye itself is the *Śiva-liṅga* consisting of the syllable *Śi*.

Because the Guru is the embodiment of mantra, the six-syllabled mantra itself has assumed the form of the six flavors— sweet, sour, and so forth; thus, because it serves as the means for the savoring of the taste of such mantra-recitation, the tongue alone is the Guru-linga composed of the letter *M*, [entering] through the two channels known as *Iḍā* and *Piṅgalā*.

Because it is the locus for the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), and because it serves as the means for practicing *prāṇāyāma*— which arises through the sequence of *recaka* and other techniques consisting of the purification of the body that is the cause for performing virtuous deeds—
the nose itself is called the "liṅga of conduct" (*ācāraliṅga*) composed of the syllable *na*. Thus...
The characteristics of the liṅga are to be understood.

Furthermore, one who possesses devotion characterized by love for the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama, as well as for those who wear the emblems of Śiva such as sacred ash and Rudrākṣa beads, and who have taken refuge in Śiva, through the realization of their essential oneness, is indeed a true devotee.
But the Great Soul, preceded by knowledge, is most firm and superior in every respect.
Affection is said to be devotion; through it liberation is attained, and not otherwise.

According to this statement in the *Śaṃkarasaṃhitā*, Maheśvara alone—who possesses the firm conviction that Śiva is indeed embodied as the Śrī-guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama—is the one who [possesses] the eight enclosures (*āvaraṇas*) characterized by the water from the feet of the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama; grace (*prasāda*); sacred ash (*bhasma*); rudrākṣa beads; and mantras.
Among the five types of conduct, beginning with internal [conduct], he is indeed ever vigilant due to his freedom from forgetfulness. When illness or similar afflictions arise,
he does not accept medicine offered to the *liṅga* except for the water used for washing the feet (*pādodaka*).

Distinguished by those two, the *liṅga* itself is the *prāṇa*, and the *prāṇa* itself is the *liṅga*; one who possesses such constant contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) is indeed a *prāṇaliṅgin*. That very *prāṇaliṅga*, having himself become the Lord (*pati*) and [the Goddess] Satī, having attained the state of being both husband and wife (*satīpatibhāva*), is the "Truth of Satī" (*satyāḥ satyam*).

Thinking "it does not exist," one abandons attachment to other women; being filled with the bliss of union with the power of one's own consciousness (*svacicchakti*), and having taken recourse to the path of renunciation (*nivṛttimārga*), one who is endowed with devotion, knowledge, and dispassion is said to be a "refuge" (*śaraṇa*).

Thus, through the cessation and manifestation of the state of such a virtuous wife and husband, and by turning away from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one becomes free from all appearances (*nirābhāsa*).

Contemplating that "all is of the nature of Śiva," one becomes unified, merged into the single Great Liṅga within, like the union of fire and camphor; thus should the stage of the limbs (aṅgasthala) be contemplated.
Here, because camphor has the nature of being an element (bhūta), and because that [element] is ultimately a product of fire (tejas).

Since the destruction of an effect consists in its persistence in the form of its cause, there is no room for the doubt that it involves the loss of its own nature. Thus, the relationship between the sixfold refuge in Śiva—beginning with devotion—and the sixfold marks—beginning with conduct—must be investigated; this is what is being stated.
The symbol of conduct, known as the sense of smell, has its locus in the state of devotion.
Endowed with the power of withdrawal (nivṛtti-kalā), it is the instrument for perceiving smell.
The Guru-liṅga, known as the tongue, is situated in the sacred place of Maheśa.
Endowed with the ritual of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), it is the means for grasping the aesthetic essence (rasa).
The Śiva-liṅga known as Netra is situated at Prasādisthala.
Endowed with the arts of knowledge, it is the means for perceiving form.
The mobile linga known as the skin rests upon the station of the Prāṇalinga.
Endowed with the digit known as Śānti, it is the means for perceiving touch.
The mark of grace known as the ear, which takes refuge in the sanctuary of the sacred site.
Endowed with the kalā beyond tranquility (śāntyatīta), it is the means for the apprehension of sound.
The mental [form] is indeed the Great Liṅga, which has its locus in the station of unity.
It is endowed with the Peaceful, the Beyond-peaceful, and the Subsequent, and is the means for accomplishing the grasping of all. Thus [it is said].

In this context, although the mind and the other organs function as instruments (*karaṇa*), they are designated as having the nature of the subtle body (*liṅga*) because consciousness— characterized by the capacity to smell and so forth— is established solely within them as the means for apprehending objects such as odors. Otherwise, there would be no distinction between the smeller and the sense of smell, nor the taster and the sense of taste.
The intended meaning is that speech would be the means for perceiving fragrance.

As for the characteristics of devotion and so forth, they are stated in the *Śaṅkarasaṃhitā* of the *Skanda-purāṇa*: "Proper conduct, devotion to Śiva, and single-minded focus on the *liṅga* and the *jaṅgama* (the living master)."
Devotion to the mark and the refuge is the unsurpassed station of the devotee.
He avoids the wives of others and the wealth of others, possessing purity of intention.
With his self disciplined through devotion to the Liṅga, he reached the great abode of Maheśvara.
One who has offered material objects to the Liṅga becomes a possessor of great enjoyments; thus the Liṅga is established.
One who avoids what has not been offered and frequents the most excellent places of grace.
The vital breath is the sign in the wind, which possesses the quality of motion; the vital breath is fully established within that sign.
There is neither pleasure nor pain, nor both; it becomes the station of the one who possesses the mark of the vital breath.
My husband is the Liṅga and I am Satī; the Lord himself is united within my heart.
There is no worldly happiness; there is no supreme place of refuge.
There are the six waves and the six states of being, and there is no eightfold worship.
The state of non-manifestation is the unification with one's own innate mark, like the union of fire and camphor.

Thus, by the statement that "in this [state] there is no worldly happiness," it is indicated that there is no taking of a wife. And so, since here the stage of the limbs (*aṅga-sthala*) is included within the stage of the signs (*liṅga-sthala*), there is the single reality of the Great Liṅga called Mahāsāda, which is endowed with the *kalā* known as Śāntyatītottarā.

The five groups of kalās residing in the remaining five liṅgas— namely, the Sādākhya-mūrti-sādākhya, the Mūrti-sādākhya, the Karma-sādākhya, and the Kartṛ-sādākhya, which together constitute the pentad of Sādākhya— when combined with these, it is the convention that there are eleven liṅga-tattvas. This being so:

The essential meaning is as follows: for the reality of the partless, compact *liṅga*, there is the *mahāliṅga*; the fivefold group beginning with *prasāda* is inward-facing and called "mental" (*mānasa*); the outward-facing fivefold group consists of those beginning with *sādākhya*, which have the alternative names *Īśāna* and so forth. Now, furthermore, of that...
In the playful manifestation of the gross phenomenal world (*sthūlaprapañca-nirmāṇa-līlā*) of Maheśī,

by virtue of the *nivṛtti-kalā*— which is synonymous with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) residing in the *ācāra-liṅga*— there arise the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which constitute the fundamental cause of the twenty-three principles (*tattvas*) beginning with *ahaṃkāra* and ending with the earth element (*bhūmi*).

The principle of Māyā, which is another synonym for the nature of the Self (ātmaprakṛti), arises. Within that, consciousness itself, having entered into the qualities (guṇas) such as sattva and the rest, is designated by the names Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā.
Fire, Sun, and Moon are sequentially contained within this.

Furthermore, there are the four castes known as Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. Since it has been stated by the Blessed One himself, "The system of the four castes was created by me according to the division of qualities and actions," one should not raise the objection: "How can the four castes arise from the three qualities? [For] Rudra is superior to the universe.
The great sage (maharṣi) is indeed the Person (Puruṣa), Rudra, according to the Vedic revelation, "Rudra is the Great Being, salutation to him";

and because he resembles pure crystal, the origin of the Brāhmaṇas consists of those who have become portions of the Great Sage Rudra, whose nature is consciousness entered into the quality of sattva.

Due to the quality of *sattva*. Because the quality of *rajas* is mixed with it, from the *sattva* portion contained therein arises the Vaiṣṇava Kṣatriya; from the *tamas* portion contained therein arises the Vaiśya who has become a portion of Brahmā; and from the quality of *tamas*, etc., arises the Śūdra who has become a portion of Indra. Other gods are of mixed origin (*saṃkara*). Thus it has been said.
And in the Parāśara Upapurāṇa it is said: "All the gods shall become Śaṅkaras, and Indra shall become a vṛṣala."
The Grandfather (Brahmā) is indeed a Vaiśya; Hari is the supreme Kṣatriya;
and the Lord Rudra is the Brāhmaṇa, the highest of all.

"The Brahminhood of Rudra, who has become Brahman, is certainly not born of a cause. If it is objected: "How can the stated meaning be established, given that it is recorded everywhere in the Purāṇas that Viṣṇu is *sāttvika* and Rudra is *tāmasa*?"—the answer is no, because regarding Viṣṇu and Rudra...

Because the designations "sāttvika" and "tāmasa" are applied based on the limiting conditions (upādhi) of preservation and destruction, Viṣṇu is by nature tāmasa and Rudra is indeed sāttvika. This has been stated in the Bhāgavata itself:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of Prakṛti; the Supreme Puruṣa, though distinct from them, assumes these here."

"Stability and the rest have the names Hari, Viriñci, and Hara"—thus [it is said]. O Girītra, that supreme light which is not accessible to Viriñci, Vaikuṇṭha, or Surendra—the lord of all the worlds—wherein there is neither rajas, nor tamas, nor sattva, and which is Brahman devoid of all differentiation; thus [it is said] in the first verse here.

Through the ornament of sequence (*kramālaṃkāra*), it is clearly perceived that Viṣṇu’s quality of being *sāttvika* and Rudra’s quality of being *tāmasa* are caused by their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of protection and so forth.
This is evident in the words spoken by Brahmā to Rudra during the occasion of the [consuming of] the Kālakūṭa poison: "O Girīśa, these [qualities] do not belong to you."

By means of this sequential ornament (*kramālaṃkāra*), the inherent nature of Vaikuṇṭha as characterized by the quality of darkness (*tamas*) and that of Rudra—also known by the synonym Surendra—as characterized by goodness (*sattva*), is perceived; for Rudra is white in color and Viṣṇu is black in color. Regarding this point, in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Whiteness..."

One should know in brief that passion (rāga) is born from the quality of sattva, attachment (rajas) is born from the quality of rajas, and blackness (kārṣṇya) is born from the quality of tamas. He whose body consists of sattva that has fallen into illusion (māyā) possesses the quality of tamas.

"He who possesses darkness (tamas) as his manifest body and the quality of sattva for the sake of the protection of the three forms (trimūrtis), he is Rudra and no other. This is because it is so recorded in the Smṛti. Herein, [all beings] from Brahmā down to an insect...
The *sakala* (embodied) is stained by the three impurities (*trimala*); Viṣṇu is the *pralayākala*, possessing two impurities because he is devoid of *kalās* during the dissolution;

Rudra is indeed the *vijñānākala*, ever-knowing because he is devoid of *kalās*; and [Īśvara] is stained by the single impurity of *māyā* for the sake of withdrawal. But the light of the limbs of renunciation extends to the upper limit.
Because he is distinguished by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the *kārma* impurity, he is called a *mantra*;

because he possesses the appearance of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhoga*) yet is characterized by the orientation toward the destruction of the latent impressions of the *kārma* impurity, he is called a *mantreśvara*;
and because he has attained the state of the destruction of the latent impressions of the *kārma* impurity, which is the appearance of the limbs of yoga (*yoga*), he is called a *mantramahēśvara*.

Thus, these are the six kinds of subjects (*pramātṛ*). However, the manifestation of the partless, compact *liṅga* consists of the vibration of the full "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃsphuraṇa*), in which the arousal of impurity has not arisen; this is the distinction. Herein, that which has entered into the category of the effects of *māyā*—whose nature is primarily characterized by difference in the form of mutual exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*)—is [the state of] *aṅga*.

It should be understood that "vaṃ" refers to the number twenty-five. Herein, it should be known that the triad of internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) and the five organs of cognition (jñānendriya) are the effects of *sattva*; the five organs of action (karmendriya) are *rājasa*; and the five subtle elements (tanmātra) and the five gross elements (bhūta) are *tāmasa*.
In this regard, because of the Lord's statement, "At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in Me," it is only some rare individual who,

through the power of virtuous deeds such as the worship of Śiva accumulated over many births, and by the grace of the Guru's glance in this very life, attains such knowledge of Brahman in its six aspects (ṣaṭsthala-brahmajñāna) and is liberated.

It must surely be so. Now, for one who has taken refuge in the Brahman characterized by the six sites as previously described, the six syllables of the *akāra*—namely *go*, *pyā*, *sa*, *dyā*, *ṣaṇmukha*, and *samuditajyotirbindu*, *ardhacandra*, *kuṇḍala*, *daṇḍa*, and *tāraka*—become the six elements themselves and attain the status of its limbs (*aṅga*). Thus it is said.
Then, upon that pedestal, one should firmly install the sixfold *iṣṭaliṅga* in the form of the *praṇava*;

the *ācāraliṅga* in the *khaṇḍikā* enclosure; the *guruliṅga* in the circular area; the *jaṅgamaliṅga* at the *gomukha*; the *prasādaliṅga* in the place of the *yoni*; and the *mahāliṅga* in the *golaka*.
Thus, because these six kinds of signs (*liṅga*) are manifest,

the devotee first, with faith and devotion, takes a fragrant substance in the hand of a well-purified mind and, while recollecting the *nakāra* mantra, offers it at the entrance of the sense of smell (*ghrāṇendriya*) to the sign of conduct (*ācāraliṅga*), which is endowed with the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).

Having become an enjoyer of that grace, he becomes one who undergoes transformation. For Maheśvara, through steadfast devotion to the Guru-liṅga endowed with the power of knowledge, having taken the substance of nectar with his well-disposed hand,
while recollecting the mantra beginning with the syllable *ma*, and having offered it into the mouth of the organ of taste, accepts that grace.

He becomes transformed. However, one who partakes of the *prasāda* of the Śiva-liṅga— endowed with the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)— having received the physical substance with a hand free from egoism through careful devotion,
while recollecting the *śikāra-mantra*, offers it at the gateway of the sense of sight and, having become an enjoyer of that *prasāda*, [attains liberation].

He becomes transformed. However, the *prāṇaliṅgin*, having grasped the object of touch with his hand while recollecting the mantra in the form of speech (*vākāramantra*), offers it to the gateway of the sense of touch belonging to the mobile *liṅga* (the body) which is endowed with the power of orientation (*aunmukhyaśakti*), and thus becomes an enjoyer of its grace.

He becomes transformed. But the seeker of refuge, through the bliss of devotion toward the *prasāda-liṅga* endowed with supreme power, grasps the meaning of the word with the hand of right knowledge; recollecting the mantra beginning with the syllable *ya*, he offers it into the opening of the organ of hearing and partakes of that grace.

One becomes transformed. As for oneness: by means of the hand of true being, through devotion to the state of *samarasa* with the Great Liṅga endowed with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), having taken up the object of satisfaction and, while recollecting the *praṇava* mantra, having offered it at the mouth of the mind, one becomes transformed, being satisfied by its grace. For one who has thus offered [it], [the result follows].
O Goddess, because she rests in the Brahman which is the object of refuge, the syllable *oṃ* is her face, and the two words *namaḥ* are her two arms.
The letter Śa is in the middle of the body, while the two letters Va and Ya are in the two feet.
The seat (pīṭha) is said to extend from the feet up to the knees; that which reaches up to the navel is called the middle.
It should be circular up to the heart, and likewise shaped like a cow's mouth up to the throat.
The throat of the *liṅga* extends to the middle of the eyebrows; the head is the top of the *liṅga*.

Because of this statement, since even that body has the nature of a *mantra-liṅga*, there is indeed nothing at all that needs to be performed. Nevertheless, the manner in which the identity (*sāmarasya*) of the *liṅga* and the limbs (*aṅga*) is to be contemplated must be understood. For instance:

Earth, having become the limb of Bhakti, becomes dissolved right there, because it is of the nature of the support of consciousness (*ciddhṛti*). Water, having become the limb of Maheśvarī, is dissolved right there, because it is of the nature of the nourishment of consciousness (*cidāpyāyana*). Fire, having become the limb of Prasādā, is dissolved right there, because it is of the nature of the radiance of consciousness (*cidujvalana*). Wind...

Having become the limb that embraces the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is dissolved right there, because its nature is vibration characterized by autonomy. Having become the limb that is the refuge of the void (*vyoma*), it is dissolved right there, because its nature is the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*). Indeed, the drop (*bindu*), which consists of the latent impressions of the object of knowledge, having become the limb of unity—
He is absorbed right there. Thus, because the devotee has the *ācāra-liṅga* as his limb, he is absorbed right there;

because [the devotee] has the *guru-liṅga* as his limb, he is absorbed right there in Maheśvara; because the *prasādī* has the *śiva-liṅga* as his limb, he is absorbed right there; [so too is] the *prāṇaliṅgī*.
Because he has become a limb of the mobile liṅga, he is dissolved right there; because Śaraṇa has become a limb of the grace-liṅga (prasādaliṅga), he is dissolved right there;
and because Aikya has become a limb of the great liṅga (mahāliṅga), he is dissolved right there—thus it should be contemplated.
Then, the conduct-liṅga merges into the guru-liṅga; the guru-liṅga into the Śiva-liṅga;
the Śiva-liṅga into the mobile (jaṅgama) liṅga; the mobile liṅga into the grace-liṅga (prasāda-liṅga); the grace-liṅga into the great liṅga (mahā-liṅga);
and the great liṅga becomes one with the dense liṅga (ghana-liṅga), which is nourished by the undivided awareness of Being.
It exists eternally, because the six marks consist of the process of reflecting the consciousness and bliss.

It should be reflected upon that such a state of identity (*sāmarasya*) between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga* is not possible according to the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*), because the sixfold objects of knowledge—beginning with the mind and ending with the earth—are false, being the effects of ignorance (*avidyā*). Only one who possesses knowledge of these six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) is truly supreme; and it has been said:
In the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā.
Animals are superior in intelligence to worms, insects, and moths.
Humans are superior even to animals; among them, the twice-born are the most excellent.
Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; among the Brahmins, those whose intellects are fixed on the sacred rites.
Among those who act with the intellect of the seasons, the renunciants are superior.
Among them, the wise are superior; among the wise, those who worship Śaṅkara are the best.
Among them, O fortunate one, the most excellent are those who are united with my own body as their liṅga.
One who possesses knowledge of the six stages (ṣaṭsthala) becomes superior among those whose limbs are joined with the Liṅga.
Therefore, there is nothing superior to him at any time throughout the three worlds.

Thus, regarding this matter, one should not suspect that a Brāhmaṇa’s wearing of the *liṅga* is unscriptural; for it has been stated in that very same [text] that "the mantra on the hand shall be a purifier," according to the scriptural determination, and because it is heard in the scripture: "We worship Tryambaka."

The summary is this: because the verbal root *yaj*—meaning "sacrifice," "worship of the gods," "forming a connection," or "giving"—implies the attainment of a connection between the *liṅga* and the body.

This is another distinction: among the sciences concerning the universe composed of the thirty-six principles described above, the Śruti is supreme; within the Śruti, the Rudraikādaśinī is supreme; and within that, the five-syllabled mantra is supreme, for two syllables therein are "Śiva. This is according to the statement of the Paurāṇikas regarding the two syllables "Śi-va."

Because [the soul] is the jewel of living beings (*jīvaratna*). Furthermore, the manner in which it is included therein must also be investigated. If it is asked, "Since the enumeration of those principles (*tattva*) is impossible without their specific definitions (*asādhāraṇalakṣaṇa*), how can the manner of their inclusion be investigated?", it is replied: regarding the principles of the signs (*liṅgatattva*) mentioned here...
Because the [categories] called Sādākhyas are mere names, because the Kalās consist of the aspect of reflective awareness (vimarśa),
and because the Liṅgas are contained within the aspect of light (prakāśa), it is of that very single form. And thus,
it is augmented by reflective awareness.
Brahman alone, for the sake of his own play, through his divine sport (līlā),
[manifests] Śiva, Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā, Māyā, Kalā, Vidyā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, Puruṣa, Prakṛti, Ahaṃkāra, Buddhi, and Manas.

It is divided into thirty-six principles (*tattva*), consisting of: hearing, skin, eyes, tongue, nose, speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
To explain: from the supreme cause, which is beginningless, endless, tranquil, and auspicious (*śiva*).

"The power of will (icchā-śakti) has emerged first; from that, knowledge (jñāna); from that, action (kriyā). From these two, the elements and the fourteen worlds were produced"—so it is stated in the Āgamas. Action constitutes one half [the right side], while the other half is knowledge; the equality between these two is the intermediate will. Will alone [is the source].
Root-joy, through its internal and external movement, is indeed the root of knowledge and action here, like the root of a sprout.

Thus, because of the established state of the *mātṛkācakra-viveka*, the very first exertion of Maheśvara, who is oriented toward creation, having entered into a portion of knowledge that is internal to his own power of will (*svecchā-śakti*),
is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) for the future manifestation of the world of moving and non-moving beings.

The Śiva-tattva is characterized by being omniscient, the creator of all, blue-throated (Nīlakaṇṭha), the Lord of Umā (Umāpati), three-eyed (Trilocana), and so forth. This very same [reality] is the Sadāśiva-tattva expounded in the Īśāna-mantra:
"The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings..."

"Brahmādhipatiḥ, brahmaṇo'dhipatiḥ, brahmā śivo me astu sadāśivom"—according to this Vedic passage, its meaning is as follows: "Īśāna" means the lord or sovereign of all sciences and the sixty-four arts; by this, his omniscience is expressed. [He is the lord] of all beings (*bhūtānām*) who are characterized by coming into existence (*bhavana-śīlānām*).
He is the Lord and controller of all moving and non-moving beings; by this, His status as the creator of all is stated.

He is the Sovereign of Brahmā—the Lord of those beginning with Tatpuruṣa and ending with Sadyojāta, who are the [five] faces of Śiva—namely Īśa, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, who are governed by the fourfold cosmic functions such as concealment (tirodhāna).

The Lord (adhipati) is the regulator of that [creation] by virtue of being its generator; He is the Lord of Brahman, the Lord of Brahman’s austerity, and Brahman Himself, who is augmented by supreme bliss. Śiva is the pure light, derived from the verbal root *vaś*, meaning "to shine" or "to be beautiful. Alternatively, He is the Lord (Īśvara), the sole treasury of infinite auspicious qualities.
"He is called Śiva by the virtuous who know the true meaning of the principle of Śiva," according to the statement of the Paurāṇikas;

or, Sadāśiva is one who is completely full of auspicious qualities. Alternatively, through the analysis "sat ā śivaḥ," he is of the nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), because the vowel *ā* denotes bliss (*ānanda*), due to its being merged into a single unity with the Praṇava.
Because it is perceived, that which is to be expressed by it— the letter *A*, which is a constituent part of the *praṇava*—
is perceived in reverse order within the *umā*; and its Lord, Sadāśiva, who is likewise constituted thus, may he be the bestower of grace upon me, whose heart is established in the *tirodhāna-kalā*.
It should be contemplated that this seven-syllabled Śaiva mantra shines forth as being inherent within these mantras.

This very [mantra] is the locus of rest for all sovereignty; it is merely included among the *tattvas* (categories of existence) by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) for Paramaśiva. This alone is to be worshipped by those seeking liberation; through its grace alone, one attains oneness with Paraśiva.

It should be understood that supreme liberation is characterized by the state of becoming one (lolībhāva). This very one is the Teacher of the World (jagadguru), the Lord of all sciences; he alone is the primordial teacher (ādiguru), O wise ones, for it is stated in the Purāṇas: "His disciple was Mahāviṣṇu, a great ocean of divine knowledge."

And as for the cause of the manifestation of Nārāyaṇa: it is precisely the exertion [of the Lord] when He has entered into the aspect of external form and action of His own power of will (*svecchā-śakti*); this is the *śakti-tattva*, which is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the future universe. It is the very play of this [power] in the form of the individual soul (*puruṣa*) that is Nārāyaṇa.
Now, this very reality of power (*śakti-tattva*),
having entered a state of intensification of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) which is internal to its own power of will (*svecchā-śakti*),
is like chickpeas and other legumes that have been soaked in water.

Distinct from its prior state, the *sādākhya-rudra-tattva*— which consists of the manifestation of the present universe, appearing as a sprouting tooth in its first form, and existing while veiled by its own sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) like the covering of a womb— is a portion of Sadāśiva. Now, that very *śakti-tattva*...

The principle of Īśvara (the Lord), which consists of the manifestation of the universe, remains having entered into the state of the intensification of its own power of action; it conceals this sprouted form of "this-ness" (idantā) within its own "I-ness" (ahantā), just as a refined object [conceals its raw material].

[This is] that which is called Nārāyaṇa, whose nature consists of the play of the states of Śakti, Tattva, and Puruṣa. Now, because this "thisness" (idaṃtā), which is dominated by activity, appears as being subsumed within the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) which is the very form of consciousness, the identity between "I-ness" and "thisness" is established— according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves— through the dissolution of the duality based on division.
This is the *śuddhavidyātattva*, which is synonymous with *tattvabrahman*.
That is to say, it is the stainless consciousness (*nirmalasaṃvitti*) obtained through the Guru and the scriptures.
Now, this very *śuddhavidyātattva*, by way of the analogy of the juice within a fruit, [resides] within those things that are dissolved inside itself.

When entities are oriented toward the process of manifestation (*bhavana*), the *māyā-tattva* comes into being, characterized primarily by the cognition of difference based on mutual non-exclusion (*anyonyābhāva*). As stated in the scripture: "The Goddess, the seventeenth *kalā*, has within herself all moving and non-moving things. Previously, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), this entire universe was undifferentiated from Māyā within the Supreme Lord.

And from the statement in the *Parāśaropapurāṇa*: "It exists in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone, not as a non-entity, by virtue of being non-different from its own cause called Māyā," [it follows that] from the Supreme Lord,
within whom all moving and non-moving things are dissolved, [the world arises] through the application of wood [as fuel].

Like the manifestation of sparks from a fire, that light which, being differentiated by the power of His will (*icchā-śakti*), enters the *māyā*— defined as above— by way of reflection, becomes the *puruṣa-tattva*. This is because, due to its separation from the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) who is autonomous light, it is overcome by *māyā*.

The realization that "I am not the Lord" arises as the cognition of non-self (*anātmatā*) with respect to the self; likewise, the cognition of self with respect to the non-self, such as the body and so forth—this dyad is the *āṇavamala*. From this very [dyad] arise the *kārmamala*, which consists of the impregnations (*vāsanā*) of the auspicious and inauspicious, and the *māyikamala*, characterized by the distinction of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
And [this state] is attained. Precisely because of being fettered by these three kinds of impurities (*mala*), one is called a "transmigrator" (*saṃsārī*).

Due to this person’s separation from Maheśvara and the consequent deprivation of his sovereignty by *māyā*, his very power of agency—which was previously uncontracted—becomes the principle of *kalā*, characterized by limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtā*).
The very power of the knower, when characterized by limited knowledge, becomes the principle of ignorance (avidyā-tattva).
The very power of fullness, having attained incompleteness, becomes the principle of attachment (rāga-tattva), characterized by addiction to objects such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women.

It comes to be. Likewise, having attained both permanence and impermanence, there arises the reality of time characterized by the sequence of past, future, and present forms. Likewise, having attained both pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness, [there arises the thought]: "This must be done by me."

The reality of necessity (*niyati-tattva*) becomes the cause of restriction (*niyama*). This pentad of *kalā* and the other [categories] is called "sheaths" (*kañcuka*) in the scriptures because, by the command of Śaṅkara, they serve as the cause for veiling the unconditioned nature of this *puruṣa*.
Now, it is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) itself, pregnant with orientation (*unmukhya*), through the process of reflective resonance (*pratisphuraṇa*), that...

It is characterized by the mutual absence of self-originated knowledge and activity; it is of the nature of the manifestation of *māyā*, which bestows pleasure, pain, and delusion; it is the state of equilibrium of the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* qualities; and it is the root cause of the twenty-three principles beginning with *ahaṃkāra* and ending with the earth element.
The principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*) arises. Then, the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāra-tattva*), which is the means for the conceit "I" and "this is mine," arises.
The principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), which is the cause of determination—such as [the doubt] "Is this a post or a person?"—arises.
The reality of the mind (*manastattva*) is the instrument of conceptualization and discursive thought (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa*);

because the cognition of a person (*puruṣatva-buddhi*) is the opposite of the cognition of a post as being correctly imagined (*samīcīna-kalpa-sthāṇutva-buddhi*), it is discursive thought (*vikalpatva*).
These three, remaining within the body—

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) consists in the instrument for the discernment of objects to be felt, such as pleasure and so forth; it is characterized primarily by the power of will (*icchā-śakti*).
Then, when connected with the external body, the ear is the exclusive instrument for the cognition of sound;
the skin is the exclusive instrument for the cognition of touch; and the eye is the exclusive instrument for the cognition of form.

The tongue is the sole instrument for the cognition of taste, and the nose is the sole instrument for the cognition of smell; this pentad is called the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) because they are characterized primarily by the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
This is so because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is common to both sound and non-sound, and so forth.
Because sound and so forth are not common [to all], there is no over-extension [of the definition]. Now, speech is the cause of the act of uttering;
the hand is the cause of acts such as giving and taking; the foot is the instrument for the acts of going and coming;
and the anus is the instrument for the expulsion of digested food and waste.

The organ of generation (*upastha*) is the means for the act of discharging semen and urine; these five, because they are primarily characterized by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), are called the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
It should be understood that this group of fourteen instruments consists of the nature of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). Now...
Sound is cognizable by the ear alone; touch is cognizable by the skin alone; form is cognizable by the eye alone;
taste is cognizable by the tongue alone; and smell is cognizable by the nose alone.
In the case of these [sensory objects], there is an absence of distinctions such as resonance or phoneme, cold or heat, blue or yellow, sweet or sour, fragrant or foul-smelling, and so forth.

It is not designated by the form of that alone because it possesses the nature of a universal; rather, space (ākāśa) is that which provides room for air, fire, water, and earth, and has sound as its sole quality;
wind (vāyu) is that which possesses motion, whirling, drying, and velocity, and has touch as its sole quality; [and fire is] that which burns and cooks.

Fire possesses the quality of form (*rūpa*); and because it exists as that which ripens and nourishes crops and the like—even in the case of the cool radiance of the moon and other luminaries where there is an absence of burning—it is not subject to the fault of being under-defined (*avyāpti*). Water possesses the qualities of liquefying, floating, and refreshing, and has taste as its sole specific quality; earth has odor as its sole specific quality.

The water-principle is the support, the earth-principle is that which is to be cut and that which is to be cooked; these are called the great elements beginning with space. Within these thirty-six principles, [the principle of Śiva] is "lower" because it possesses the nature of the universe, appearing as a sprout or as one already sprouted, starting from Śiva and ending with Śuddhavidyā.

Beyond that is the *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), which conceals the reality (*tattva*). Thus, the *parāpara* (both supreme and non-supreme) is the cause of liberation; it is the fourth state (*turīya*) because it consists primarily of the notion of difference based on division—which, according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves, culminates in non-difference—because the *māyā-tattva* is the cause of bondage, and because it consists of the gross universe. It is the *apara* (non-supreme).
Because it consists of the cognition of difference based on mutual non-existence, herein,
for the Puruṣa accompanied by the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and primordial nature (prakṛti),
the twenty principles beginning with the ear and ending with the earth have entered the waking state.

Because they are denoted by the term "contact" (sparśa), the pentad beginning with Kalā has entered the state of dream; because it is denoted by that [term] due to its internal state, Māyā alone is the principle of the state of deep sleep. This is the distinction, based on its nature as delusion (moha). Now, one might object:
since the scripture states that the Self consists of twenty-five [principles], [how can this be so] given the twenty-five principles?

If it is asked, "How can there be thirty-six forms when [the categories] are limited?", the answer is no; for just as the sixteen categories are included within seven categories, so too are the six coverings (kañcukas), beginning with Māyā, included within the covering of Māyā, since they are effects of Māyā. And thus, the five elements, beginning with earth, are included within the category of *kalā*. Furthermore, the three—namely, the *guṇas*, *niyati*, and *rāga*—are included within *vidyā*.
