Because [the group] beginning with Māyā and ending with Niyati are included within the Puruṣa as its "sheaths" (kañcukas) and are thus contained therein;
because the fourfold group beginning with Prakṛti and ending with Manas constitutes the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
and because Prakṛti is synonymous with Citta; [and likewise for the organs] beginning with the ear and ending with the organ of procreation.
Because the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) consist of the phonemes that are his knowledge and action;

because the five gross elements (*bhūta*) constitute his body; because the pentad beginning with Śiva is denoted by the sibilant (*ūṣman*) phonemes; because the sibilants are of the nature of power (*śakti*); and because powers have the supreme Śiva as their essential nature.
The discernment is that there is no contradiction, because it is of the same nature as that [pure consciousness], being of the form of its own pure contemplation.

The universe, consisting of these thirty-six principles, is either Śiva called the Praṇava, or the Praṇava is of the nature of Śiva; for as it is stated in the Purāṇas: "The distinction between the signified and the signifier is never entirely separate," and according to the Vedic revelation: "Śadā-śivo-m."

O Goddess, the Lord of Heroes (Vīrendra) exists as the one who has simultaneously pervaded the entire circle of the three worlds; such is the determination of Śambhu. The letter *A* is the foremost of all phonemes, the supreme light, and Śiva himself.
The letter *I* is the final [phoneme], whose form is *kalā*, and is celebrated as being called "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*). Of these two—

"Because of the scriptural statement, 'From the form of the state of identity (samarasa), [it is] indeed "I," the stainless one,' and because of the Vedic revelation, 'I am the first-born,' and so forth, [the universe] is condensed through a state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya)— according to the analogy of the fluid within a peacock's egg— into Śiva, whose singular embodiment is the primordial *praṇava* and who consists of the nature of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). For instance, in this term 'Śiva'..."

Since the four classes of phonemes (*varṇa*) are manifest, and according to the position of the *Triṃśikā-śāstra* the letter *va* denotes the principle of *māyā*, the thirty-one principles ending with *māyā* and the letters from *ka* to *va* that denote them are all included within the letter *va*.
Because the thirty principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *bhūmi* are their effects, and because it has been stated that there is a tetrad of *dhāraṇās* for air, fire, water, and earth,
there is the tetrad of principles beginning with *śuddhavidyā* and ending with *śakti*, as well as the letter-group *śa*, which denotes them.

Since it has been stated that [the letter *śa*] is included within *śakāra*, and that following it is the well-known group beginning with *śa* (the *śādi*), preceded by the five Brahmans (*brahmapañcaka*); whereas in the vowel *a* resides the Sadāśiva-tattva, which is complete with the sixteen digits (*kalā*) consisting of the nature of grace (*anugrahātmaka*).
And the sixteen vowels, which denote those digits, are contained therein.
When the letter *ī* is situated upon the head of the letter *śa*, the power (*śakti*) that constitutes its instrument shines forth.

Since the letter *ī* is established as the Will (*icchā*) among the powers of the six vowels beginning with *a* (Anuttara), one should contemplate the universe as the Supreme Śiva— the form of the blossom of the wish-fulfilling tree of the non-duality of Śiva.

Likewise, here too in the word "aham" (I), the letter *m* denotes the principle of the Puruṣa (*puruṣatattva*). For it has been stated: "O observer of good vows, the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Puruṣa reside respectively in the consonant groups beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*. Thus, the principles up to Māyā are included within Puruṣa; [and] Puruṣa...
For it is sung [in the Gītā]: "Established in Prakṛti, one indeed experiences the qualities born of Prakṛti. Everything else is as before.

But the power that has become the cause arises from the letter *ha* alone, because that [letter] signifies *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), as has been demonstrated in that manner. Likewise, this applies here in the case of *oṃ* as well, because it consists of the forms of the letters *a*, *u*, and *m*.
Because the letter *u* has been revealed in the *Triṃśikātattvavivaraṇa* as being subtle in nature like the letter *ha*,

the rest is as before. Thus, because it rests in the single meaning "I am Śiva" (*oṃ śivo 'ham*), and because it takes the form of a compendium of the *mātṛkā* and is based on scripture (*śrauta*), it also serves to establish Maheśvara.

Because it is the nature of the Great Mantra (Mahāmantra), one who desires liberation must possess such an internal realization; for the Śruti declares: "Only by knowing Him does one become immortal here. Thus, in the sequence described, [one should contemplate] the six stages (ṣaṭsthala) of the Brahma-sūtras, which establish the consciousness consisting of vision and action as affirmed in the Śiva-sūtras.

One who possesses full knowledge of the great mantra of the thirty-six principles of Brahman becomes immortal in this very life and in this very body. Although conducting oneself like an ordinary person through food, worldly dealings, and so forth, one is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) due to the absence of future births. After the fall of the physical body (*piṇḍapāta*), [one attains final liberation].
Indeed, through the expansion of the powers of omniscience and so forth, one becomes directly liberated. Now, since this mantra is included within the *Puruṣasūkta*, prior to this—

If it is asked, "How can the stated meaning be established, given that the consciousness whose nature is vision and action, the Brahman of six planes, the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), and the Great Mantra have not been attained?"—[the answer is: "The Thousand-eyed One" (*sahasrākṣa*); for [the Vedic verse says]:
"Having encompassed the earth on all sides, He stood beyond it by ten fingers' breadth."

Because it is stated in scripture: "And he is the lord of immortality; such is his greatness, yet the Puruṣa is even greater than this," [the text demonstrates] through the manifestation of his thousand eyes the power of cognition (*jñātṛtā-śakti*); and by the word "lord" (*īśāna*), the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) characterized by being the agent of worldly existence and liberation through both immanence and transcendence is shown. Such is his greatness...
Because by the word "mahimā" (greatness) both the insentient and the living— characterized respectively as knowledge and action— are included within the independent consciousness,
and because it is stated that [the Lord] is "greater than this," [it follows that] the consciousness of the supreme Śiva consists of the nature of vision and action.

"This very autonomy is the Self; therefore, He is the Supreme Śiva"— according to this position established in the *Śivasūtravārtika*, because [the universe] has that as its sole purpose, and because of the Vedic scripture stating "all beings are one foot of Him," and because the thirty-six principles are included within that, [it follows that] "three feet of His are the immortal in heaven."

Since it is stated in the Śruti, "The Puruṣa rose above with three feet," and because the Great Mantra of the Brahman of the Six Stages has been attained, for one who possesses such reflection, even mere conversation constitutes *japa*.

The very engagement in that [practice] is the vow (*vrata*); for it has been indicated by Śiva that "discourse is recitation (*japa*), and the engagement of the body is the vow. Therefore, because everything is endowed with the four syllables of Śiva, it is auspicious (*śivam*).
Thus,

[this is] the blossoming [of the lotus of the heart] through the spreading rays of the nectar of the poetic utterances of the moon-like lord of sages, Nāthānandamuni— the teacher of the knowledge of Brahman— [who is] fully nourished by the play of the equilibrium between duality and non-duality, characterized by the aesthetic harmony (*sāmarasya*) of Śrī Prakāśa and Vimarśa.
This *Śivādvaitamañjarī*, composed by the joy of its own radiance within the heart-lotus buds of those who possess discernment,
has reached completion; like the moonlight of the full moon, it triumphs exceedingly as it spreads delight across the hearts of the connoisseurs.
May there be well-being and prosperity.

sthala (Brahman).
The stage of the Linga (the Lord), the stage of the Anga (the individual soul),

The stage of the chosen liṅga,

Īśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Virāṭ, Prājña, Taijasa, Viśva.
The site of the Great Liṅga, the site of the Grace-Liṅga, the site of the Moving Liṅga,

the site of the Conduct-Liṅga, the site of Unity, and the site of Refuge.

Power, the energy of power, devotion, and the power of devotion.
The power of consciousness (cicchakti), the supreme power (parāśakti), the primordial power (ādiśakti), the power of will (icchāśakti), the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti),

Avadhāna-bhakti, naiṣṭhika-bhakti, śraddhā-bhakti,

Ūṃ, obeisance to the illustrious Reṇukācārya.
Now begins the section on the Pāśupata doctrine entitled *Śaivasiddhāntadīpikā*.
I bow to, praise, and take refuge in the Lord who is devoid of color and form, yet who is free from being devoid of color and form, and who speaks of color and form. (1)

Salutations to that enemy of Tripura, by whom the universe— consisting of the moving and the unmoving— is woven like warp and woof on all sides, and by whom the distinction between the individual soul (paśu) and its bonds (pāśa) is destroyed.

In this context, first of all, this gross body— which is the locus for pride regarding birth, family, and so forth— is a composite of earth, water, fire, air, and ether. Within it, there are those who possess a fixed lifespan and bear the castes such as Brāhmaṇa and others in accordance with their prior merit and demerit, as well as physical beauty, prosperity, and the keenness of the senses.

And these experiencing selves become possessors of fixed enjoyments. For each individual self, there exist thirty principles—beginning from the earth-principle up to the principle of *kalā*—which constitute the equipment for experience and have been brought forth since the commencement of creation; these are [manifested] individually and extremely subtly through karma within each respective self.

At the end of the attained lifespan, having abandoned the previous body, it will take up another body like a caterpillar moving from one blade of grass to another; the self (*ātman*) is the substratum of the merits and demerits performed by that [body], distinct from the body, consisting of knowledge and action, eternal, formless, and all-pervading.

The transmigrating person (puruṣa) is bound by the fivefold fetters consisting of the powers of obstruction: those of the individual (āṇava), the karmic (kārmika), the illusory (māyīya), the lunar (baiṃdava), and the power-natured (śaktyātman).
If it is asked what the principles (tattvas) are that constitute his subtle body, which serves as the apparatus for experience:
These five elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—have been described.

If one asks what their cause is, it is the pentad of pure existence (*sanmātra*). These are: the principle of smell (*gandha-tattva*), the principle of taste (*rasa-tattva*), the principle of form (*rūpa-tattva*), the principle of touch (*sparśa-tattva*), and the principle of sound (*śabda-tattva*). This group of ten is called the effect (*kārya*).

The five organs of action (karmendriyas) are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ; their respective functions are speaking, walking, grasping, excretion, and sexual pleasure. The five organs of perception (jñānendriyas) are the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose; their respective objects are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Of this...
It has been stated that the pentad beginning with speech and the pentad beginning with hearing constitute the instruments (karaṇa).
Furthermore, this triad consisting of the mind (manas), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the intellect (buddhi)—
unlike the sense organs such as hearing— does not perform its function by emerging externally from this body.

Because it resides within the interior space of the body and initiates activity, these three are called the "internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa). Furthermore, they perform the conceptualization of objects and the engagement of the sense organs, such as hearing, with their external objects.

The function of the mind (*manas*) is volition. The functions of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) are self-conceit, imagination, and the impelling of the vital airs such as *prāṇa*. Determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the function of the intellect (*buddhi*); this refers to the ascertainment that "this is indeed silver, not mother-of-pearl. Thus, the twenty-three principles (*tattvas*) have been previously mentioned.

From the principle of *buddhi*, which serves as the cause for determination (*adhyavasāya*), the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense) arises, distinguished by its divisions of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*. Here, from the *sāttvika* *ahaṃkāra*, the mind (*manas*) and the five organs of perception (*jñānendriya*), such as hearing and the rest, arise. Here...

From the *rājasa* ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the five organs of action, such as speech and the rest, are born. Here, from the *tāmasa* ego, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) beginning with smell are produced. From this pentad of subtle elements, the five gross elements (*bhūta*) are born. And [this is] *dhāraṇā*.

The functions of the five elements are: aggregation, combustibility, the joining together of parts, and the providing of space for the other four elements. Among these, sound, touch, form, and taste are the common qualities of earth.

Odor is the specific quality [of earth]. Sound, touch, and color are the general qualities of water, while taste is its specific quality. Sound and touch are the general qualities of fire, while color is its specific quality. Sound is the general quality of air.

Tangibility, however, is a non-common quality. For ether, sound is its only quality; this sound is not of the nature of articulated phonemes (*varṇa*), but is an echo. The causal principle for the twenty-second principle, the intellect (*buddhi*), is the principle of the qualities (*guṇatattva*). And this is designated as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
Having become threefold, it sequentially becomes the cause of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

The cause of this *guṇatattva* is the *prakṛtitattva*; the *guṇatattva* is the twenty-fourth principle (*tattva*), and the *prakṛtitattva* is the twenty-fifth principle. Within both of these principles—
It has been established that the effect of the *prakṛti-tattva* is the *guṇa-tattva*. The effect of the *guṇa-tattva* is its state of being the cause of pleasure, pain, and delusion,
as well as its being the sequential cause of the twenty-three principles beginning with the internal organ (*buddhi*), which are distinct from itself.
The twenty-five principles beginning with the *pṛthivī-tattva* and ending with the *prakṛti-tattva* are named the "impure path" (*aśuddhādhvan*).

Above this is the *rāga-tattva*; its function is the instilling of desire in the self for objects born of *prakṛti*. Above that is the *niyati-tattva*; its function is [the determination] of the self by means of each respective [object].
The rule is that actions performed must be experienced by the self alone.

Following this is the principle of Time (*kālatattva*); its function is the delimitation of the person's experience, such that one experiences for a long time or experiences for a short time. Beyond this is the principle of Knowledge (*vidyātattva*); its function is...

The *kalātattva* (principle of limited agency) is that which perceives the intellect (*buddhi*), colored by objects, within the *puruṣa*; its function is to remove a portion of the innate impurity (*mala*) of the self’s power— which is like the natural blackness of copper— since beginningless time.

The manifestation of the nature of the Self has *māyātattva* as its cause. The production of the previously mentioned *prakṛtitattva*, *rāgatattva*, and *vidyātattva* occurs within *kalātattva*. The production of *niyatitattva*, *kālatattva*, and *kalātattva* occurs within *māyātattva*.

The five principles of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *kāla*, *niyati*, and *rāga* are called the "five coverings" (*pañcakañcuka*). Because the nature of the person (*pums*) who is veiled by these is [limited] consciousness, it is designated as the "principle of the person" (*puruṣatattva*) due to the existence of impurity (*mala*). Therefore, the self possesses a nature that is insentient (*jaḍa*).
The five principles beginning with *rāga-tattva* and ending with *kalā-tattva* are called the mixed path (*miśrādhvan*).
These constitute thirty-one principles. Within each individual self, there exist distinct subtle bodies (*sūkṣmadeha*).
These are the substrata for these effects—the worlds and bodies.
There are thirty common principles (*tattvas*) that serve as the substrata for all worlds and possess the nature of the universal self.
The cause of all these is the impure *māyā-tattva*. This *māyā-tattva* is eternal, all-pervasive, and bound by the karma of all individual selves through its own functional activity.

Although it illuminates knowledge and action, it is delusive; beyond this is the thirty-second principle, the *vidyā-tattva*, and beyond this is the thirty-third, the *īśvara-tattva*. Within this *śuddhavidyā-tattva* reside seventy million great mantras.

The twenty-eight *saṃhitās* beginning with the venerable *Kāmika*, the eight lords of the *gaṇas* beginning with Nandin who are worshipped according to the *Siddhānta-śāstra*, the world-protectors beginning with Indra, and their weapons such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and so forth, all reside [there]. In the *Īśvara-tattva* are the *Vidyeśvaras*.

The eight [deities] beginning with Ananta exist. Among these, Ananta, because he is the Lord of all, is the sovereign over those Vidyeśvaras who dwell in the Vidyātattva, as well as others; he is the agitator of Māyā and the creator of the worlds and principles belonging to Māyā. Furthermore, this one—

Distinct from the Supreme Lord and possessed of a single impurity (*mala*), one becomes graced by the Supreme Lord through the ripening of that impurity; by this process of manifestation, those within the mass of souls designated as *pralayākalas*— who possess both the atomic (*āṇava*) and karmic bonds (*kārmabandha*)— and who have reached the ripening of their impurity, [attain liberation] by means of the supportless [grace] alone.
There are one hundred and eighteen Rudras favored by the Supreme Lord. Among them,
the Rudra named Śrīkaṇṭha is the creator of the worlds within the principles (tattvas) below the principle of Prakṛti at the conclusion of the intermediate dissolution.

Among the multitude of souls known as *sakala*, who are bound by the threefold bondage consisting of the *āṇava*, *kārmika*, and *māyīya* types, he becomes distinguished through knowledge, yoga, austerity, study, and so forth,
and becomes the sustainer of the stations of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. At the time of the intermediate dissolution (*madhyapralaya*), this [soul]...
Abiding in the principle of *rāga*, when the time for emanation arrives,
he stands as the presiding authority over the emanations of Brahmā and Viṣṇu prior to the creation of the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*),
and [over] the lords of the worlds below that, the thirty-three million deities, and the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*).

Brahmā creates the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), consisting of the fourteen worlds, which serves as the dwelling place for all living beings. Among the previously mentioned Rudras, the Śatarudras—remaining within the element of earth alone, apart from the five-elemental cosmic egg—become the protectors of the cosmic egg. [This occurs] within the principle of the *guṇas*.
The venerable Lord Rudra, remaining together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
having exercised his authority until the end of the intermediate dissolution (madhyapralaya), and having withdrawn these two, Brahmā and Viṣṇu,
himself [abides] in the principle of Miśrādhvarāga.

And the deity Vīrabhadra exists together with him. On the head of Prakṛti there are eight, and on the head of Kalā there are eight; Śrīkaṇṭha and Vīrabhadra, along with the hundred Rudras—thus, one hundred and eighteen Rudras are embodied beings graced by the Supreme Lord.
They become [liberated], untouched by the maintenance, creation, and knowledge associated with the stations of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
through the power of yoga and knowledge whose agent is the Self, they attain the stations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others.
This occurs for these one hundred and eighteen Rudras due to the ripening of their impurities and through the grace of the Supreme Lord.

The attainment of the [spiritual] station occurs gradually, preceded by initiation (*dīkṣā*). For those residing in the principle of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyātattva*), the attainment of the station results from the ripening of their impurity (*mala*) and the grace of the Supreme Lord. The essential nature (*svarūpa*) of these Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) is *baindava* (pertaining to the point), while the body of the one hundred and eighteen Rudras is *māyīya* (pertaining to Māyā).

The body of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others is composed of primordial matter (prākṛta); however, like the essential forms of the eighteen hundred Rudras and the Vidyeśvaras, all the forms of the Supreme Lord himself are to be meditated upon in worship and other rites. [This applies even] to the body of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

Because he is primordial (*prākṛta*) and because [his state] cannot be attained even through the grace of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the Supreme Lord is not meditated upon by anyone, unlike the bodies of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. Both the station of Brahmā and the station of Viṣṇu constitute the level of the bound soul (*paśubhūmi*). Both the station of Rudra and the station of Īśvara constitute the level of the master (*patibhūmi*). Above this principle of Īśvara—

The Sadāśiva-tattva; beyond that, the Śakti-tattva; and above that, the Śiva-tattva. This triad of tattvas serves as the basis for the designations of authority (adhikāra), enjoyment (bhoga), and dissolution (laya) belonging to the Supreme Lord.
Within this triad of tattvas, there are no entities distinct from the Supreme Lord.
There exist no other selves that function as agents.

Those who possess faith— practitioners initiated through the initiation of a seeker (sādhaka-dīkṣā)— become enjoyers after reaching their respective worlds by the grace of the Supreme Lord, having attained the states of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority.
Whether abiding until the limit of detachment (*vairāgya*) or until the limit of the great dissolution (*mahāsaṃhāra*),
the liberated selves (*cidātmānaḥ*) do not become like the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvaras*). In the principle of knowledge (*vidyātattva*),
there are fifty letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.

The twenty-eight compendia, beginning with the *Kāmika*, exist in the form of *vaikharī* speech within the principle of Īśvara, as does the *praṇava*. In the principle of Sadāśiva, there is the *bindu* together with all its parts, and the *nāda* together with all its parts. In the principle of Śakti, the seed of the intellect (*buddhi*), which has the subtle object as its referent, having become distinct within each individual self, [manifests].
The subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), consisting of the essence of the subtle channels (*nāda*), remains; it is the cause of the *śivatattva*, as well as the *bindu*.
There is no designation of a distinction between the principles (*tattva*) for the *bindu* and the *śivatattva*.
Of Śiva, who abides presiding over the principles of Sadāśiva and Śakti, there are the forms *sakala* (with parts) and *sakalaniṣkala* (partially without parts).

The names are Niṣkala (the partless), Vyakta (the manifest), Vyaktāvyakta (the manifest-unmanifest), Avyakta (the unmanifest), Maheśvara (the Great Lord), and Sadāśiva (the eternally auspicious). Among these thirty-six principles (*tattvas*), *bindu* is eternal, all-pervasive, formless, the constant substratum of the Supreme Lord, consisting of both sound and meaning, and [the means] for the selves through *nāda* and other stages.

It is the cause of right knowledge and is free from delusion. The path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) consists of all things other than *māyā*, beginning with the principle of earth—which is insentient—and extending up to Śiva, comprising thirty-six principles. Beginning from the world of Kālāgni...

The path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*) consists of two hundred and thirty-five worlds, beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Bhuvana. The path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) consists of the fifty phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*. The path of words (*padādhvan*) consists of eighty-one mantras whose essence is the *vyomavyāpin*.
The eleven paths of mantra consist of the forms of the primary cosmic egg (mūlabrahmāṇḍa). They possess the five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti.
Among these, the three paths consisting of kalā, tattva, and bhuvana are material (dravyātmaka);
the three paths consisting of varṇa, pada, and mantra are of the nature of sound (śabdarūpa). Within these, the path of bhuvana—

It exists by relying upon the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*). The path of the principles, the path of the energies (*kalādhvan*), and the three paths consisting of phonemes, words, and mantras exist in relation to the worlds and the body.
The supreme cause of these six paths is the reality known as Kuṇḍalinī and Pure Consciousness (*śuddhavidyā*).

And it is also called Brahman. These six paths constitute the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of souls; distinct from the six paths, [the souls] are eternal, all-pervading, conscious, different in each body, impure, performers of action, enjoyers of the fruits of action, and possessors of limited knowledge.

The selves are agents of some action and possess a Lord. Due to their various types of bondage, these are said to be of three kinds: *sakala* (with parts), *pralayākala* (inactive due to dissolution), and *vijñānākala* (inactive due to pure consciousness). For these selves, the bondage pertaining to *māyā* consists of the categories (*tattvas*) beginning with *kalā* and ending with *pṛthivī*, as well as the worlds (*bhuvanas*), cosmic abodes (*bhauvanas*), and so forth.
The bond of desire (*kāmyabandha*), produced by acts such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice or the killing of a Brahmin, takes the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as *apūrva*;
it rests upon the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) situated within the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) and results in fruits consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
The bond called impurity (*malabandha*) obscures the knowledge and action inherent to the true nature of the selves (*ātman*).

Having become distinct within each individual self, it becomes eternal, pervasive, and an insentient substance, endowed with manifold powers, intending to pervade at the end of its own time. This "atomic" (baiṃdava) bond is the cause of the bodies of the Vidyās, the Vidyeśvaras, and others.

And the bond (*pāśa*), consisting of the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*), is the cause of all sounds ranging from the subtle (*sūkṣma*) up to the manifest speech (*vaikharī*) that constitute the apparatus for the enjoyment of transmigratory existence called "the whole" (*sakala*);
it is also the cause of the beginningless attributes of the fourfold bonds of *māyīya*, *kārmāṇava*, and *baidava*.

Śiva-śakti itself is called "bond" (pāśa) by way of metaphorical designation. For those abiding on the pure path (śuddhādhvan), there are only two bonds: the atomic (baiṃba) and the obstructive power (rodhaśakti). For those abiding on the mixed path (miśrādhvan), however, there are four bonds: these two, along with the atomic (āṇava) and the karmic (kārmika). For those abiding on the impure path (aśuddhādhvan), there are likewise these four.

Thus, there are five types of bonds, including the *māyīya*. Among these three which reside within the path (*adhvan*), for those dwelling in the Pure Path (*śuddhādhvan*)—who are like the liberated—there is only unsurpassed bliss;
they are untouched by suffering, and pleasure, pain, and delusion do not exist for them. For this reason, it is designated as the "Pure Path."

However, for those dwelling on the mixed path (*miśrādhvan*), even though they possess omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), pleasure, pain, and delusion also exist. For this reason, this is called the "mixed path. For those dwelling on the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*), however, there is limited knowledge (*kiṃcijjñatva*), limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*), and pleasure, pain, and delusion. Therefore...

For this reason, it is called the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*). Herein, the *baindava* and *māyīya* bonds (*pāśa*) are adventitious (*āgantuka*). The *kārma* bond, however, is beginningless by way of its continuous flow (*pravāha-anādi*) and serves as the means for the experience of fruition (*bhoga*).

The *āṇava* bond, on the other hand, is beginningless in its primordial state (*kūṭasthānādi*); at the conclusion of its own maturation, [it is dissolved] through that which consists of the grace of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-prasāda*).

The bond of karma is to be removed by initiation; otherwise, it is exhausted through knowledge, yoga, renunciation, or experience. These means, beginning with knowledge, are attained through the scriptures, and those scriptures are of five kinds.
It is of five kinds: worldly (*laukika*), Vedic (*vaidika*), spiritual (*ādhyātmika*), super-pathway (*atimārgika*), and mantra-based (*māntrika*).

The worldly consists of treatises such as Āyurveda and Daṇḍanīti, which have visible results. The Vedic, however, refers to that which, based on the ritual portion (*kriyābhāga*) of the Vedas, was composed by seers (*ṛṣi*) to establish merit such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and to achieve goals such as heaven.

This is the treatise on the sciences (*imāṃsāśāstra*). Regarding the Veda, the two treatises composed by the sages—Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika—which examine the categories (*padārtha*) and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as proofs for its human authorship:
these three together constitute the treatise that yields both visible and invisible fruits.
The internal [science], however,

consists of those treatises composed by sages with the fruit of self-knowledge as their goal, directed toward the Upanishadic portions known as Sāṃkhya, Pātañjala, and Vedānta. As for the science concerning the path beyond [the world] (atimārgika):

The Pāśupata, Kāpāla, and Mahāvrata systems were promulgated by Rudra; however, the Siddhānta scripture was promulgated by Śiva as a mantra. The venerable Jaimini is the author of the Mīmāṃsā scripture; by means of this scripture—

The meaning being established is as follows: the definition of a sentence, the Vedas being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), the manifold world being eternal, that rites such as *iṣṭa* and *pūrta* must be performed,
and that the performance of ritual action alone is the means for the performer to attain heaven and other rewards.
They maintain that the selves are distinct from the elemental body and senses, that these selves are many, and that there is no Lord (Īśvara) who is different from them;
however, the subject matter propounded by the Vaiśeṣika system consists of earth, water, fire, and air.
The four elements are impermanent; their causes are distinct atoms (paramāṇu) bearing their respective names; there is another cause of sound, eternal, consisting of the fifth element, space (ākāśa);
and other than these are the eternal time (kāla) and the directions (diś).

The selves (ātman) are distinct from the elements, causes, body, and sense organs; they are formless and eternal. There are many selves. Furthermore, there is an eternal mind (manas), distinct from these [others], which is the cause of cognition and so forth.
Thus, there are nine substances (dravya): earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind—each being designated as such within its respective self.

The category of substance (*dravya*) is distinct from these; the category of quality (*guṇa*), such as color and so forth, is other than this [substance]; the category of action (*karman*), such as upward throwing and so forth, is different from that [quality]; the category of generality (*sāmānya*), such as "cowness" and so forth, is other than that [action]; the category of inherence (*samavāya*), such as "whiteness is here in the jar," is other than these five. It is distinct from these five.

Regarding the category of *viśeṣa* (particularity): among these six categories, knowledge arises from the contact of the mind with the reality of the self (*ātman*). From this, the performance of actions consisting of merit and demerit arises;
from this, the performance of actions consisting of sin arises; and from this, the body and the sense organs [arise].

The attainment of heaven and hell occurs by the power of merit and demerit; God is the sustainer of all this. From the conjunction of God with the mind, there arises knowledge and so forth, but knowledge is not produced [as an effect]; rather, knowledge is established by its own nature. Thus [is the description] of the six categories of entities.

The destruction of karma occurs through the knowledge of similarity and dissimilarity; without the knowledge produced by the conjunction of the mind [with the self], beings remain like stones, and this alone is liberation— thus say the Vedas, which have God as their author.

Furthermore, the subject matter to be established by the Nyāya-śāstra is as follows: the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, are to be known for the sake of establishing the objects of cognition (*prameya*); these sixteen categories (*padārtha*) are exactly according to the sequence stated by the Vaiśeṣika; the definition of liberation (*mokṣa*) is of the manner thus described; and [the existence of] God (*īśvara*).
Furthermore, the one who impels knowledge, desire to act, and effort regarding the true nature of categories is eternal;

these two authors of the respective treatises are Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda. However, the subject matter propounded by the Sāṃkhya system is [the self] which is eternal, all-pervading, and insentient in nature.

The cause of all things is this *prakṛti*, which is formless and a state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; and this *prakṛti* is also known as the twenty-fourth *tattva*. Its effects consist of the twenty-three *tattvas* beginning with the *buddhi-tattva* and ending with the *pṛthivī-tattva*.

Distinct from these twenty-four principles (tattvas) are the selves (ātman), which are eternal, all-pervading, formless, manifold, devoid of both omniscience and omnipotence, and consist of pure consciousness alone.
Thus is the system of twenty-five principles; and within the body composed of the five elements, it is indeed the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva) [that constitutes the self].

The primary principle (pradhāna) possesses an essential nature that is without distinction in both the state of liberation and the state of worldly existence, and it is devoid of impurity; yet, by the power of beginningless ignorance residing in the intellect (buddhi), the knowledge of worldly pleasure and pain arises.

Kapila is the author of this treatise [the Sāṃkhya], which holds that liberation results from the destruction of ignorance through the knowledge of the distinction between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*), and that there is neither a self distinct from these nor a Lord (*īśvara*). However, the subject matter presented by the Pātañjala-śāstra (Yoga) is as follows: thus, both primordial nature and its evolutes...

The self, bondage and liberation, discriminative knowledge, yoga, and the requisites of yoga—these constitute the twenty-six principles; the Lord is the one [additional] principle. His distinction from these selves consists in his independence, his power of creation, his designation as "mind" (citta), and his maintenance of the form of pure sattva alone.
And Patañjali is the author of this treatise, which also teaches the knowledge of the Self.

As for the subject matter propounded by the Vedānta system, there are four types of Vedāntins: the followers of Bhāskara, the proponents of Māyā (Māyāvādins), the proponents of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahmavādins), and the proponents of the Playful Brahman (Krīḍābrahmavādins).

Among these, the followers of Bhāskara [maintain that] the entire mass of entities—gods, humans, animals, and so forth, consisting of both the insentient and the sentient—is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman. This [Brahman] is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), all-pervading, and it alone is the Lord (*īśvara*).
Due to ignorance regarding its state of being subject to modification, the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) revolves; yet this [Lord] is indeed one alone.

From the perspective of ultimate truth, because these transformations are indeed transformations, the nature of the self— which appears distinct from the body through the knowledge of Vedānta— is realized as being none other than the Supreme Brahman; this is what is to be known as liberation.
And the proponents of illusion (māyāvādins) maintain that while the previously mentioned supreme Brahman alone is the ultimate reality,
this entire world— deceptive and false— is an illusory material cause, like silver appearing upon a real mother-of-pearl shell.
Brahman is neither unreal like a rabbit's horn, nor is it real like [an ordinary object].
They maintain that liberation consists in the self-realization of the nature of Brahman— which is distinct from illusion— through the knowledge of Vedānta.

The proponents of Śabdabrahman, however, maintain that the supreme Brahman, which is the cause, becomes identical with sound during the state of being an object of knowledge. They teach that all things—whether insentient or sentient, perishable or imperishable—are in reality transformations of this [Brahman], and that in essence they are nothing but sound; thus, the realization that its very nature is such is liberation.

But for those who maintain that Brahman is a player (*krīḍā-brahmavādinaḥ*), it is the very Brahman previously described who thinks, "I am alone; I shall become many and sport in various ways with manifold objects of transformation produced by myself," and thus becomes many. That manifold object is eternal; that is the real entity.
Vyāsa is the author of these systems of thought, which establish that liberation is attained through direct realization by oneself.
There are six schools of philosophy: Mīmāṃsā, Vaiśeṣika, Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Pātañjala, and Vedānta.
Among these, the Vedic ones consist of the Vedānta alone as the non-dualistic (advaita) scripture, while the other five are dualistic (bheda) scriptures.
Apart from this group of six, there are non-Vedic, nihilistic (nāstika) scriptures.
If one asks what those scriptures are, they are three: the Buddhist, the Jain, and the Materialist (Lokāyatika). Among these—

However, the doctrine propounded by the Lokāyatika treatise is as follows: "Only earth, water, fire, and air are real; the collection of these alone constitutes the body, which is the self. This knowledge of the self increases when the body grows and diminishes when the body decays. Thus, there is no such thing as Īśvara.
Is anything seen? Only pleasure and pain are seen; heaven and hell exist only as long as the body lasts.

Once the body is destroyed, there is no such thing as an unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) to be performed. For this very reason, some maintain that there is no self (ātman) apart from the body, for it is not seen.
This refers to Bṛhaspati, the author of the Lokāyata treatise.

However, according to the Buddhist scripture, the meaning being established is as follows: there are twenty-three principles (*tattvas*) beginning from the earth-principle (*pṛthivītattva*) up to the intellect-principle (*buddhitattva*). Among these, the intellect-principle is the primary one.
Within the body composed of the five elements, the intellect-principle alone constitutes the self (*ātman*); that indeed is the primary principle.

Starting from this principle of consciousness (*buddhi-tattva*) and extending downward, the entire aggregate of objects is momentary; otherwise, neither a permanent self nor a Lord exists. The teacher of this scripture is the Sugata alone, who is to be venerated. Liberation, however, is the cessation of the stream of ignorance that is experienced as impermanent, like a flowing current of water.
Some maintain that, in the absence of the contact with pleasure and pain, there would be only a continuum of pure consciousness;
others hold that liberation is simply the destruction of the continuum of ignorance, just as a lamp that proceeds step by step perishes when its oil and wick are exhausted. These...
There are four schools: the Sautrāntikas, the Vaibhāṣikas, the Yogācārins, and the Mādhyamikas.

Among these, some maintain that the entire aggregate of objects is unreal and that only the continuum of consciousness is real; others demonstrate that while this entire aggregate of objects exists, it is nevertheless momentary.

However, the doctrine propounded by the Ārhata-s is as follows: the author of the Ārhata scriptures, the Arhat himself, is an eternally perfected soul (*jīva*); there exists some entity accompanied by defects such as beginningless delusion;
and there are other sense organs as well—all of this exists together with these very names, along with the body.

It should be expressed by the words "there is no body. Regarding these categories of things, there is only non-violence; it should be expressed by the words "there is no body. Through knowledge of the scriptures spoken by the Arhats, through the ascetic practices taught in those scriptures such as lying on heated stones, and through the non-violence of the Jinas—of this [it should be expressed].

The faults are destroyed. Thus, like an Arhat, one becomes one whose faults are exhausted. Furthermore, when asked whether these scriptures exist or not, they are not declared to either exist or not exist; these three [points] are outside the Veda. Some say there is a Lord (Īśvara), while others say there is no beginning, stability, or [a creator], and those devoid of proper conduct are nihilists (nāstika).

They are said to be the six Vedic sciences (*veda-śāstra*). Among them, the four Vedas—namely the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, *Sāman*, and *Atharvan*—are their source; these [others] are their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*).

The six sciences— metrics (chaṃdas), ritual (kalpa), phonetics (śikṣā), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta), and astronomy (jyotiṣ)— as well as the exposition of the duties of the social classes (varṇadharma) such as the Brahmins and the duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma) such as studentship (brahmacarya), are presented in the form of mantras, in the form of Brāhmaṇas, and in the form of injunctions (vidhi), along with the Upaniṣadic portions.

The eighteen Dharmaśāstras, beginning with those of Manu, are the authorities that establish the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti), the individual soul (puruṣa), and the Lord (īśvara) as the objects of knowledge in the Vedas; they are the promoters of the conduct established by the Vedas, and the regulators of practices such as ritual purity, social transactions, and expiatory rites. Their authors are—
The great sages, such as Manu and others,

[hold this view]; however, the reality established by the *Pāñcarātra* scripture composed by Vāsudeva is the twenty-fifth principle (*tattva*), which stands above the twenty-four principles consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*) and the principles taught in Sāṃkhya— namely, Vāsudeva.
Thus, there is no supreme reality (paratattva) that possesses a name;

from this supreme reality, four emanations—Kṛṣṇa, Aniruddha, Makaradhvaja, and Rauhiṇeya—are produced for the purpose of creating the world. By these four, the entire universe, consisting of both the insentient and the sentient, [is manifested].
And as it has been stated by the proponents of the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavādins*) in the Vedāntas, all this is indeed Vāsudeva.

In the Vedas there are no goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), whereas in the Pāñcarātras the goals of human life do exist. Therefore, having initiated [the disciple] according to the procedure taught in the Pāñcarātra and having propitiated Vāsudeva, [one should abide] in the very nature of Vāsudeva.

And [the statement] "laya is liberation. Furthermore, the subject matter being propounded by the Itihāsas and Purāṇas [concerns] both the Vedic dharmas and the principles set forth in the Sāṃkhya and Pātañjala systems.
It is the exposition of the subjects taught in the Pāñcarātra, Pāśupata, and Śaiva scriptures; of creation and dissolution; of the genealogies; of the Manvantaras; and of the dynastic histories.
The Itihāsa is the Mahābhārata, and the Purāṇas are eighteen in number. The author of these is Vedavyāsa.
"The twenty-fifth principle is the Self (ātman), the twenty-sixth principle is Rudra,
and the twenty-seventh principle is Śiva; having known these categories of reality, one becomes liberated through initiation"— this is the essential meaning of the Purāṇas.

However, the subject matter propounded by the Pāśupata Śāstra is as follows: there are many selves (*ātman*), which are all-pervading, eternal, produced through the conjunction of cause and effect, mutually distinct from one another due to knowledge,
and while they possess no *āṇava* impurity, they are bound by the *māyīya* impurity and the bond of karma (*karmapāśa*).

Experiencing the pleasures and pains of saṃsāra until the arising of dispassion, the quality of knowledge of the Supreme Lord becomes transferred to those selves who have been initiated according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures. Like householders renouncing the world after entrusting the burden of their families to their sons, the Lord, having transmitted self-knowledge [to them], [withdraws].
He ceases from his own office. However, the matter being established by means of the Great Vow (mahāvrata), according to the sequence taught in the Pāśupata [tradition],
concerns those selves who are liberated from the impurities consisting of the atomic (āṇava), the karmic (kārmika), and the māyīya [impurities], even while they are in the state of transmigration.

It is indeed the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and not the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) [that liberates]; those initiated according to the sequence taught in the scriptures, who wear bones and perform the conduct prescribed by the scriptures, become liberated. And those liberated ones possess only the power of knowledge. As for the pair of powers, knowledge and action—
"Of the one Supreme Lord alone. However, the meaning being propounded by the Kāpālika is that,
according to the sequence set forth in the Great Vow (mahāvrata) of the Pāśupatas, there exists both the definition of the self and the definition of bondage.

Furthermore, it is said by the exponents of the scriptures of the Pāśupata Mahāvrata and Kāpāla traditions that one who has been initiated according to the sequence prescribed in their treatises must, day after day, wander for alms in a human skull toward a direction pervaded by the single banner and flag of equanimity (*sāmya*), and there he should eat; and that for them, as for those of the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*), liberation is attained.
The three Rudras residing in the principles of Māyā and Vidyā—
namely Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta— were appointed by the Supreme Lord here in this world to inspire faith in the Śāstra of the Siddhānta, which had not been seen before.
When the isolation of consciousness (*vijñānakaivalya*) is favored by the four downward-facing [faces],
there are four downward-streaming scriptures (*adhaḥsrotas*) declared by these four selves (*ātman*) known by those names, consisting of the Gāruḍa, Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, and Bhūta.

It is stated that according to the Gāruḍatantra, the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is to be worshipped after meditating upon His Tatpuruṣa aspect as being identical in nature to Brahman. By means of this scripture, mantras and medicinal herbs for the direct treatment of snakebites have been taught. According to the Dakṣiṇatantra, however, [one should worship] Aghora.

It is stated that the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is to be worshipped after meditating upon Him as being of the very nature of Brahman; furthermore, it is said that the Supreme Lord is to be made manifest through yoga, and there are also applications of mantras for the sake of victory over enemies. According to the Vāma-tantra, however, one should meditate upon Vāmadeva as being of the very nature of Brahman.

It is stated that for the purpose of subjugating women, the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) is to be worshipped, and the mantras, tantras, and medicinal herbs [for this purpose] have been taught. Furthermore, according to the Bhūtatantra, one should meditate upon Sadyojāta as having the nature of Brahmā and worship the Supreme Lord for the sake of treating spirits, ghosts, and demons.
The Śākta Tantra was taught by a certain soul residing within the principle of Śakti (śaktitattva), who employs mantras and medicinal herbs.
Like the Vedāntic doctrine of Bhāskara, this system holds that everything—both insentient and sentient—is a transformation of Śakti; these constitute the four lower currents (adhassrotas).
The scriptures beginning with the *Kaula* were directly proclaimed by Śiva.

Other scriptures, such as the *Mānava*, were spoken by human perfected beings (*siddhas*) such as Maccheṃdranātha and others. For those who possess the knowledge of the Lokāyata, [reality] arises from the knowledge of the four elements—earth, water, fire, and air—which constitute that very principle.
Birth ceases. For the Buddhists, the production of the phenomenal world from the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) ceases.
For the Jains, the birth of principles below the principle of qualities (*guṇa-tattva*) ceases.
For the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, the essence of saṃsāra ending at the principle of intellect ceases. For the Sāṃkhyas—

Even though there is knowledge of the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, because it is impossible for them to possess knowledge of the reality of the objects on the mixed path beyond *prakṛti*, there is no destruction of all karma and thus no liberation through knowledge; according to the Pāñcarātras, the cycle of transmigration ceases prior to *prakṛti*.

For the Vedāntins, there would be the attainment of the principle of Puruṣa; for the Paurāṇikas, there would be the attainment of the principle of Rāga; for the Kāpālikas, there would be the attainment of the principle of Kāla; for the Pāśupatas, there would be the attainment of the principle of Māyā; and for the Mahāvratas, there would be the attainment of the principle of Vidya.

For those initiated into the *Śrotontara*, *Gāruḍa*, *Dakṣiṇa*, *Vāma*, and *Bhūta* Tantras, there shall be the attainment of the worlds (*bhuvana*) of Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti, which reside within the *Śakti-tattva*.
For those who are purely *Śākta*, there shall be the attainment of the *Śakti-tattva* itself. [This applies also] to the scriptures of the *Kaula-yāma* and so forth.
Due to the occurrence of attachment to violence and sexual intercourse, one may attain the state of a *piśāca*.
However, the Siddhānta scripture is twofold, consisting of the divisions of Śiva and Rudra;
this follows after the transformation of *bindu-śakti*, which consists of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *praṇava*.

Of the ten Śivas— known as Māyā, Ūrdhva, and Vijñānakevala— who are born from the Mātṛkā, are composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter beginning with the Praṇava, and are graced by the Supreme Lord, [the scriptures] are designated by the names Kāmika and so forth.
Thus, there are ten scriptures called the Śiva-bhedas, which were proclaimed from the two faces of Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva, whose nature consists of sound and meaning.
In this way...

There are eighteen scriptures known as the *Rudrabheda*, which were proclaimed by the mouths of the eighteen Rudras— Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna, and the others— who had been instructed in knowledge by the Supreme Lord, and which bear names such as *Vijaya* and so forth.
Thus, with each of the twenty-eight scriptures numbering one hundred million [verses], there are twenty-eight times ten million verses;
this is the name of the Siddhānta of these twenty-eight scriptures.
Each of these consists of four quarters: Jñāna (Knowledge), Kriyā (Action), Yoga, and Caryā (Conduct).
By means of the "Knowledge" (jñāna) limb among these, however, one [learns] the nature of the Supreme Lord,

as well as the nature of the selves— the Vijñānākala, Pralayākala, and Sakala— and the nature of the fetters consisting of the individual (āṇava), karmic (kārmika), and māyic (māyīya) bonds, along with the power of obstruction (rodha-śakti) which is of the nature of limited agency (baiṃdava), and the nature of Power (śakti).
Furthermore, the manner of the creation of the thirty-six principles (tattvas), beginning from the principle of Śiva down to the principle of Earth,
must exist as the means for the experience of individual souls;
and the nature of the worlds and the lords of the worlds, beginning from the Supreme Lord, [must likewise exist].
The extent of these [worlds] in yojanas, their measurements,
the nature of the dissolution at the base, the intermediate dissolution, and the great dissolution,
as well as the manner of creation following each respective dissolution.

Furthermore, the exposition of the Pāśupata, Mahāvrata, and Kāpāla scriptures is presented by setting forth their respective doctrines as prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), and the determination of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is proclaimed.

By means of the *Kriyāpāda*, however, the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*), the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyāvandana*), worship (*pūjā*), recitation (*japa*), and fire-oblations (*homa*) are taught.
The specific commitments (*samaya-viśeṣa*), the nirvāṇa-consecration (*nirvāṇa-saṃskāra*), the master-consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*),

the practitioner-consecration (*sādhakābhiṣeka*), and initiation (*dīkṣā*)— which serves as the means for the self’s enjoyment and liberation— are proclaimed. Furthermore, by the Yoga-pāda, these [are explained], as well as the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and the lords of the principles (*tattveśvara*).
The lords of the worlds, the Self, the Supreme Lord, and Śakti;
the manifestation of Māyā and Mahāmāyā, which constitute the cause of the universe;
and the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* for those who seek the realization of the principles pertaining to this world.
The methods of breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and absorption (samādhi),

as well as the locations of the foundational centers (ādhāras) such as the mūlādhāra, are explained; furthermore, by means of the Caryāpāda, expiation (prāyaścitta), the investiture of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa), and consecrations (pratiṣṭhā) are taught.
The characteristics of the Śiva-liṅga, the characteristics of manifest liṅgas such as Umāmaheśvara and others,
the characteristics of the lords of the Gaṇas such as Skanda and Nandin, and the characteristics of the rosary (japamālā) are declared; furthermore,

the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) and ancestral offerings (śrāddha) are taught, through which the attainment of the state of Rudra occurs by means of the purificatory rite of the observance (samayasaṃskāra).

Through specific refinement (*viśeṣasaṃskāra*), the attainment of the state of Īśvara occurs. Above the *prakṛti-tattva*, on the path of the mixed (*miśra*) levels, the attainment of the *rāga-tattva*—the first *tattva* in that sequence—is itself the attainment of the state of Īśvara.
This [attainment] is superior to the liberation (*mokṣa*) taught in the Sāṃkhya, Pātañjala, Vedānta, and Pañcarātra traditions, by means of the initiation into *nirvāṇa*.
It brings about liberation, which consists in attaining identity with the Supreme Lord;
and that [liberation] is twofold, being either immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇa*) or delayed liberation (*asadyonirvāṇa*).
Through initiation for immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*), they attain liberation by abandoning the body at the very moment following the ritual action.
The initiation for immediate nirvāṇa (*asadyonirvāṇadīkṣā*) consists of purifying the past elements and future karmas at the time of initiation;
then, by purifying the present karma that serves as the cause of the currently experienced body, one attains liberation through the abandonment of the body upon the exhaustion of the lifespan.
It causes [the soul] to attain [its goal]. However, the *sādhaka-dīkṣā*, even when devotion to Śiva and the worship of the Śiva-liṅga are present,
subsequently causes one who desires the status of a Vidyeśvara or other such positions to attain those respective positions.
Having attained those respective states,
if they become detached in the interim, they are liberated at that very moment; otherwise, they are liberated at the time of the great dissolution (mahāsaṃhāra).

The seedless initiation (*nirbījadīkṣā*), however, is to be performed for women, children, the elderly, the sick, and kings; for at the very time of initiation, the preceptor has already purified and performed those rites— such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and the worship of the Śiva-liṅga— which would otherwise have to be practiced after the initiation.

The initiation with seed (*sabījadīkṣā*), however, should be performed by the teachers for those sons who are capable. Through this initiation, both types of karma— those of past and future forms— as well as all bodies that have reached the state of maturation and the enjoyments of those bodies, are destroyed.

Because the actions that constitute the cause of the body must be purified, the bodies themselves must indeed experience their respective pleasures and pains; in this way, the threefold karma is destroyed. This occurs through the observance of scriptural rules prescribed until death following initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Since it has been stated that knowledge, yogas, and austerities— accomplished through means such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth— are for the purpose of purifying the impurities that act as auxiliary causes for the karma constituting the present body, liberation is not attained by these. Rather, liberation occurs only through initiation (*dīkṣā*), which consists of the grace of the Supreme Lord, and not by other means.

After the initiation (*dīkṣā*), if there is a deficiency regarding the preceptor (*ācārya*), purification from a fault committed intentionally occurs through expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Purification from the omission of mantras or ritual substances occurs through the offering of the *pavitra* thread. Purification from the unintentional omission of observances (*niyama*) occurs at the conclusion of the final sacrifice (*anteṣṭi*).
The rites that must necessarily be performed after the time of initiation (dīkṣā) are: the fulfillment of restraints (yama) and observances (niyama),
the Śaiva twilight worship (saṃdhyā-vandana), the worship of the Śiva-liṅga, the fire-ritual for Śiva (śivāgnikārya), the carrying out of the guru’s instructions,
and the worship of Maheśvara according to one's capacity.

Actions that are not to be performed [by one who has been initiated] are: eating the remains of offerings (nirmālya) from other deities, reviling Śiva, reviling devotees of Śiva, reviling the scriptures of Śiva, reviling the conduct prescribed in the scriptures of Śiva, misappropriating the property of the deity, and harming living beings; these are declared for one who has been initiated and follows the prescribed observances.
The characteristic of the liberated self is that,
being freed from the fivefold bonds known as the atomic (āṇava), the karmic (kārmya), the māyīya, the individual (baiṃdava), and the power of obstruction (rodhaśakti),
it possesses omniscience, eternal contentment, primordial awakened consciousness, and absolute sovereignty, just like the Supreme Lord.
Although these selves possess unimpeded power and infinite capacity,
they do not have the agency for creation and so forth like the Supreme Lord, nor do they possess the existence of objective bliss;
rather, the presence of attachment, aversion, and the like is the cause of their lack of agency regarding creation and the rest.

Through his fivefold activity, the Supreme Lord alone bestows supreme grace. [Thus ends the *Śaivasiddhāntadīpikā*, the most excellent of all systems. [It was composed by Sarvārthaśambhudeva and is in accord with the Śaiva tradition.]
[The Pāśupata treatise titled Śaivasiddhāntadīpikā is completed.]
